Introducción MBA 2024–2025 · Trabajo principal realizado por Jose Francisco Zubizarreta Rodriguez Este documento reúne los principales ensayos, presentaciones y proyectos entregados durante el MBA 2024–2025 en la Escuela de Negocios Judge de la Universidad de Cambridge. Se ha compilado como una referencia única del trabajo principal realizado a lo largo de los trimestres Michaelmas, Lent, Easter y Summer. Estos archivos son las entregas principales de varias asignaturas. Algunas asignaturas no requerían ensayo, presentación ni proyecto: en estos casos, el principal criterio de evaluación fue un examen final, por lo que no aparece aquí ningún trabajo escrito de esas asignaturas. Para consultar el programa completo, revise el plan de estudios en https://www.jbs.cam.ac.uk/masters-degrees/mba/curriculum/. El programa varía ligeramente de un año a otro, ya que se ajusta a los recursos y a las tendencias emergentes, por lo que las asignaturas que aparecen allí pueden no coincidir exactamente con las de este curso académico.

Reconocimiento El trabajo individual de International Finance (Finanzas Internacionales) (MBA130, entregado el 27 de junio de 2025, página 163 de este documento) obtuvo el Primer Premio del Cambridge Lanvern Prize for Best Essay in International Finance. El trabajo se redactó en formato de artículo de opinión dirigido a un público empresarial general, y el premio lo reconoce como el mejor ensayo de la asignatura. Este logro es un testimonio de los exigentes estándares de excelencia que se mantienen en el MBA de Cambridge.

Resumen del contenido Trimestre Michaelmas: trabajos individuales en Business and Sustainable Development (Negocios y Desarrollo Sostenible), Organisational Behaviour and Leadership (Comportamiento Organizacional y Liderazgo), Management Praxis I (Praxis de Gestión I) y Organisations versus Markets (Organizaciones frente a Mercados), junto con la presentación del Cambridge Venture Project (Proyecto de Emprendimiento de Cambridge) para el Arthur Rank Hospice Charity (Grupo 28). Trimestre Lent: el caso y la presentación del trabajo en grupo de New Venture Finance (Finanzas de Nuevas Empresas) (Grupo 10), trabajos individuales en Behavioural Finance (Finanzas Conductuales), Corporate Governance and Ethics (Gobierno Corporativo y Ética), Strategy (Estrategia), Negotiations Lab (Laboratorio de Negociación) y Digital Business (Negocios Digitales), y el proyecto de consultoría global de BlackRock sobre IA en el sector inmobiliario, con su informe final y diapositivas para presentar. Trimestre Easter: trabajos individuales en Strategy (Estrategia), Macro-Economics (Macroeconomía) e International Finance (Finanzas Internacionales), la evaluación grupal en Advanced Strategy (Estrategia Avanzada), y el borrador sobre si los inversores institucionales deberían aumentar su asignación al crédito privado, preparado para el Cambridge Finance Concentration Project (Proyecto de Concentración en Finanzas de Cambridge). Trimestre Summer: la presentación del proyecto Lean Six Sigma para el Centre for Endowment Asset Management, y el informe reflexivo individual sobre el coste computacional y el consumo energético de la inferencia de IA para el Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance (MBA36A).

Introduction MBA 2024–2025 · Main submitted work completed by Jose Francisco Zubizarreta Rodriguez This document brings together the main submitted essays, presentations and projects completed during the MBA 2024–2025 at the University of Cambridge Judge Business School. It is compiled as a single reference for the principal work produced across the Michaelmas, Lent, Easter and Summer terms. These files are the main submissions for several subjects. Some subjects did not require an essay, presentation or project: for these, the main grading criterion was a final examination, so no written work from those subjects appears here. For the full programme, please review the curriculum at https://www.jbs.cam.ac.uk/masters-degrees/mba/curriculum/. The programme differs slightly from year to year as it is adjusted for resources and emerging trends, so the subjects listed there may not match exactly those of this academic year.

Recognition The International Finance individual assignment (MBA130, hand-in 27 June 2025, page 163 of this document) was awarded First Prize in the Cambridge Lanvern Prize for Best Essay in International Finance. The assignment was written in op-ed form for a general business readership, and the prize recognises it as the best essay in the subject. The award is a testament to the exemplary standards of excellence upheld across the Cambridge MBA.

Content overview Michaelmas Term: individual assignments in Business and Sustainable Development, Organisational Behaviour and Leadership, Management Praxis I and Organisations versus Markets, together with the Cambridge Venture Project presentation for the Arthur Rank Hospice Charity (Group 28). Lent Term: the New Venture Finance group case write-up and presentation (Group 10), individual assignments in Behavioural Finance, Corporate Governance and Ethics, Strategy, Negotiations Lab and Digital Business, and the BlackRock global consulting project on AI in real estate, with its final report and slides to present. Easter Term: individual assignments in Strategy, Macro-Economics and International Finance, the group assessment in Advanced Strategy, and the draft on whether institutional investors should increase their allocation to private credit, prepared for the Cambridge Finance Concentration Project. Summer Term: the Lean Six Sigma project presentation for the Centre for Endowment Asset Management, and the individual reflective report on AI-inference computational cost and energy use for the Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance (MBA36A).

pages.text:
I.

Introduction

The present document provides an assessment of the potential consequences for BP (British Petroleum P.L.C.) on embracing the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Specifically, the opportunities and risks goals address in this work will be centred around how the UN Targets are related to Clean Energy, Innovation, Sustainable Consumption and Climate Action. The key decision for BP to make is whether they would benefit from expanding their deployed EV charging infrastructure and embrace SDGs based on identified opportunities and risks. Energy Provisioning for Transport has been selected as main industry for this assessment given its CO2 global impact and BP is chosen given its worldwide relevance and intention to improve its overall environmental reputation. According to a study on greenhouse emission worldwide (Statista, 2024, p.25), the global C2 Emissions in 2023 were caused by Transportation 21.11% and Power Industry by 38.24%. Based on these 2 metrics the energy provision for transport plays a significant role on global C02 emissions. II.

Motivation

The motivation for this assessment comes from 2 main drivers for BP: Public Relations and long-term commercial strategy. First, given the prevalence of the ecological impact 2010 Gulf of Mexico spill, BP as a global organisation has committed more than 69 Billion USD to compensate for the economic impact and legal settlements (BP America, 2024). More recently, BP has committed towards their given the significant discussion of climate change impact and acknowledging new opportunities for BP to improve their global image, they have publicised their sustainability commitments as shown in their Net Zero Ambition Report (BP P.L.C., 2024, p2). The second driver comes from a commercial strategy standpoint. The development of sustainable Electric Vehicles (EVs) charging infrastructure is critical to place the company in a leading position for this growing market, which in turn is linked to a significant reduction of carbon impact. According to a worldclass sustainability report (Statista, 2023, p. 12) the usage of EVs has displaced 13.1 billion litres of gasoline with a significant carbon emissions reduction. BP through a global engagement on EV infrastructure development would embrace four critical UN SDGs. III.

UN Framework in Sustainable Development

The United Nations originally defined the Sustainable Development Goals in 2015 derived from the Millenium Development Goals (MDGs). The SDGs as per the UN published references (United Nations, 2024) remained as a more specific set of meaningful targets for all its signing countries to achieve true and sustainable development across all nations, with emphasis on environmental protection and responsible economic development. This set of principles can represent a unique

6

opportunity for BP to consolidate their commitments on sustainable business practices, together with solid corporate accountability and transparency. Given the priorities mentioned in the Sustainability Report (BP P.L.C. 2023) the organisation is reinventing itself to embrace new technologies and NetZero frameworks. As acknowledged in the document, there are di erent angles to evaluate the best sustainable approach to enable this meaningful transition. By embracing four specific UN SDGs, discussed in the next section, BP will structure their sustainability and corporate actions on NetZero and green development.

IV.

Assessment on each SDG

The SDGs found to be more relevant for the Net Zero Goals and Sustainable Strategy of BP are introduced in this section based on the UN SDG main site (United Nations, 2024). Each SDG is then contrasted with the areas of opportunity and risk that each will represent to BP. SDG 7 - A ordable and Clean Energy. Under this goal the targets are defined towards renewable energy mix (target 7.2), energy e iciency (target 7.3) and global cooperation on research and development of cleaner sources of energy (target 7.a). Considerations – In order to develop a ordable and clean energy solutions for EV charging infrastructure, BP could expand its investments in o shore wind energy, in Northern Europe where the company already possesses considerable infrastructure and expertise according to their reports (BP P.L.C., 2023). The company might also explore innovative energy storage solutions, such as integrating hydrogen production facilities with its wind farms to create a more reliable renewable energy system. Additionally, they could design their EV charging network by integrating solar panels and battery storage at charging stations. This would let renewable energy to power vehicles while providing better experience for customers. SDG 9 - Industry Innovation and Infrastructure. This goal specifies the targets around infrastructure as follows: developing sustainable and reliable infrastructure (target 9.1) and using clean and environmentally sound technologies (target 9.4). Considerations – For further innovation in the EV charging domain, BP could implement smart-grid technology to optimise charging times based on grid carbon intensity and introduce mobile charging vans for emergency top-ups in remote areas. To improve the customer experience and maximise station e iciency, the company could develop an AIpowered app that predicts queue times and suggests optimal charging routes, and then partner with retailers to provide quality amenities during the charging wait time.

7

SDG 12 - Ensure sustainable consumption and production patterns. This goal primarily is focused on guiding multinational organisations to adopt sustainable practices and integrate sustainability data into their reporting processes (target. 12.6). Considerations – The company can enhance sustainable consumption and production patterns through several targeted initiatives. For instance, they could significantly increase their investments in renewable energy sources as suggested in the previous paragraphs. And gradually reducing their traditional oil and gas operations. This transition should be working together with more e icient production processes that reduces waste and environmental impact across their existing operations, including the adoption of carbon capture and storage technologies. BP could improve its approach to solar energy by developing cutting-edge solar technologies integrated with smart grid systems and use the continuously growing windfarm infrastructure deployed across Europe and USA. SDG 13 - Climate Action. This goal emphasises the climate changes measures to be implemented strategically and with thorough planning (target 13.2). Considerations – BP can take climate action e orts by strategically expanding its EV charging network, particularly focusing on rapid-charging hubs at existing petrol stations and working with local authorities to install chargers in urban areas with limited o -street parking. The company should prioritise powering these charging points with renewable energy as previously exposed in the other SDGs using renewable energy sources. Meanwhile, it is possible to implement a dynamic pricing model that encourages o -peak charging to reduce grid strain. Additionally, integrating digital solutions that allow drivers to easily locate available chargers and pay seamlessly would help accelerate EV adoption, consequently furthering BP's contribution to emissions reduction.

V.

Analysis of Sustainability Challenges and Opportunities

Government Guidelines Opportunities – Both in North America and Europe there are ambitious guidelines and policies from their respective governments to maximise the deployment of EV infrastructure. For instance, in UK, the NetZero Mandate (UK Government, 2024) specifies that by 2030 80% of all new vehicles need to be running on non-fossil fuels. Similar initiatives are defined in USA and mainland Europe (Statista, 2024). Risks – Political environments can lead to a diminishing interest to provide su icient support on the EV journey adoption, hence compromising the value of the returns on the investments to be done by BP on charging infrastructure. For instance, are strong changes on the UK government support on EV infrastructure according to the ruling party (Godar, 2024). Nevertheless, the overall commitment to remove fossil fuel dependency is a long-term objective as reported by the global emissions report (Statista, 2024). 8

Growing Market of EVs As reported by Statista (2023, p9) the global market of EVs is growing significantly, leading to a consistently growing demand for charging infrastructure. It is expected to quadruple in size between 2021 and 2025. Opportunities – With the previously mentioned growth, there is a solid justification on investing on further infrastructure, with a significant increase on revenue through the respective energy provisioning. Risks – According to Statista (2023, p9) there is still range anxiety, upfront costs and lack of charging infrastructure that can prevent the EV charging points market to grow as expected. BP, together with its competitors, EV manufacturers and governments need to collaborate to mitigate these risks and manage driver expectations accordingly. Renewable Energy Supply It is important to note that renewable energy sources need to be provision proportionally to the growth of EV infrastructure planning. It is claimed that EVs generate 66% less of carbon emissions compared to their fossil fuel counter parts (Local Government, 2024). Opportunities – There is good availability of renewable energies that BP can already connect to their supply grid as per the current number of chargers. This in turn can leverage additional technologies as explored in the SDG 7 subsection, for enable solar panels to be collocated with the charge points and reduce losses on electricity transmission through the grid. Risks – There is a clear challenge on whether renewable energy supply would scale by 20x as it is potentially the expected increase once most of the EV charging points will be deployed in the upcoming future. Absence of su icient renewable energy supply would lead to the need for additional dependency on coal, gas, nuclear energy and waste incineration to compensate. Consequently, the emissions of the EVs could significantly grow or become close to the emissions of the fossil fuel powered vehicles. Competition Currently, Shell aims for 90% of drivers to be within 10 minutes' drive of a Shell rapid charger by 2030 (Shell U.K. Limited, 2024). BP needs to react and plan with respect to their main competitor accordingly. Opportunities – Competitors as Shell are moving quickly towards deploying a large infrastructure for the provision of energy and deployment of charging points across US, Europe and UK at an aggressive pace. BP can aim to catch up at a similar pace considering similar goals of been very close to most of the drivers in these developed countries.

9

Risks – As infrastructure will need to grow by at least one order of magnitude, there are significant challenges on setting up the equipment in the right locations and ensure that there is not an oversupply in particular areas and undersupply in other areas. Furthermore, talent could be constrained due to the required amount of training and compensation required for a solid maintenance force serving this infrastructure.

VI.

Connection to other sustainability frameworks

Natura is a successful global cosmetics company headquartered in Brazil. Although their industry di ers from BP, still their corporate governance can bring significant light on sustainability and accountability practices to BP. According to public article on Natura (Centre for Climate Engagement Climate Governance, 2023), they have introduced the Integral Profit and Loss Methodology that accounts on collecting data across P&L reporting focused on environmental and social impact. Their methodology can easily be implemented by BP to quantifying the environmental e ect of the SDGs and EV energy provisioning previously discussed. Another relevant methodology, on validating the full NetZero accountability to be reported by BP is the concept of Regeneration. As described in the Stanford Social Innovation Review (Marquis, 2024), regeneration consists of letting natural cycles to let the planet replenish the resources we have consumed. This is illustrated with a renewable energy organisation located in Vermont, with unique market and regenerative mechanisms to generate carbon o sets and decrease financial di iculties. In the context of BP, regeneration together with Integral P&L methodologies, can lead to ensure BP can certify their energy sources to be fully renewable and regenerative. These methodologies in turn lead to a fully integrated NetZero approach on EV energy distribution. One final remark, in terms of potential global sustainability recognition, BP can aim to set the example for their peers and adjacent industry players. There is a 2025 Global 100 is a ranking on sustainability (Corporate Knights, 2024). Their energy methodology quantifies metrics such as the energy use vs the renewable energy generated by a company. Aiming to be ranked top by the Corporate Knights, would let BP to fully go ahead with the NetZero strategy for their EV charging infrastructure, and embrace again the SDGs.

VII.

Strategic Recommendations

Based on the previous analysis, BP should scale up their EV charging infrastructure. Despite the challenges and risks mentioned before, the investment presents a big strategic opportunity. The global shift towards transport electrification, assisted by governmental policies and growing EVs demand, suggests that companies such as BP must adapt their business models to remain relevant in a rapidly evolving energy 10

landscape. BP's existing supply chain of renewable energy resources is a key advantage to serve the expanding EV market. The company's established brand recognition, aided by its deep expertise in energy distribution, places it in a good position to capture a significant share of the EV charging market. The integration of EV charging infrastructure would also complement BP's broader strategy of diversifying into renewable energy, helping to future-proof its business against declining fossil fuels demand (Statista, 2024). VIII.

Conclusion

Despite challenges such as grid capacity constraints and scaling renewable energy supply chain, early investment in EV infrastructure could lead to substantial long-term benefits. By establishing a larger presence in the EV charging space, BP can build better global reputation, embrace UN SDGs, and potentially influence industry standards. To do so, BP needs to: 1) quantify their EV charging energy supply with Integral P&L; 2) validate their energy sources Regeneration; and 3) aim for the highest levels of sustainability recognition as illustrated with the Corporate Knights ranking. Furthermore, the company can leverage its expertise in global energy distribution and mitigate the risks derived from competition, change of government EV incentives, changes on EV demand and renewable energies supply. This will lead to a more sustainable and resilient business model for the time to come. References BP America (2024) Gulf of Mexico commitment. I.

Introduction and Motivation

One of the most challenging scenarios to drive a massive organisational and cultural change is the digital transformation through AI of Retail Banks around the world. Their structure is one of the most complex to drive any major transformation due to their legacy hierarchical and regulation structures (Arnold, 2014). Better customer experience can counteract the declining reputation and perception of banks as illustrated by a reputational scenario in the UK (Lawrence and Stiles, 2018). It is claimed that financial organisations can leverage big data, AI and open platforms to drive innovation and remain competitive as financial institutions (Schatt, 2014). For instance, challenger Banks (those lacking physical branches and large physical offices) represent a menace to the status quo of the conventional banks. Several tech-innovation actions from retail banking have taken place since the mid-2000s. Since then, all around the world there have been innovation driven banks with a very cost-effective structures running on free and open-source technologies (Tapscott, 2006). Subsequently, during the 2010s-decade, banks started embracing new technologies as AI to optimise their operations (Chishti, 2020). Now with GenAI, banks around the world are expected to increase their spending from 6 Billion USD in 2024 to 85 Billion USD in 2030 (Statista, 2025). There is no doubt that there is a massive need to revolutionise the banking sector and become more digital and AI driven. However, as discussed during our Organisational Behaviour and Leadership course, a major change like transforming to a digital bank requires not only resources to be invested but a major shift of organisational culture (Stiles, 2024). My motivation for this work stems from my experience as Head of AI and Digital Transformation at one of the largest banks in the UK. Besides the heavy investment and technology, there were several challenges to deliver that transformation for such a financial institution. II.

Challenges to Embrace AI

The experience I had to enable AI in the retail banking sector, is well summarised by the query below which is followed by my assessment on how to overcome the respective challenges. ChatGPT-Query: Provide-a-200-word-maximum-assessment-of-work-culturechallenges-to-drive-AI-transformation-in-a-financial-institution. "Transforming a financial institution through AI requires overcoming significant work culture challenges. Resistance to change is a primary obstacle, as employees accustomed to traditional workflows may be reluctant to embrace AI-driven systems. This resistance often stems from fears of redundancy or skill obsolescence, compounded by a lack of understanding of AI's role in augmenting rather than replacing human capabilities. 14

Siloed departmental structures pose another barrier. Collaboration between data scientists, IT professionals, and business units is essential for successful AI implementation. However, entrenched hierarchies and fragmented communication channels can hinder the cross-functional alignment needed for AI projects to thrive. The institution's risk-averse nature, while essential for regulatory compliance, can slow innovation. Strict adherence to existing policies may stifle experimentation and the iterative processes critical for AI development. Balancing compliance with flexibility is a delicate but necessary task. Moreover, leadership may lack the strategic vision or technical expertise to advocate for AI adoption effectively. Without strong advocacy and a clear articulation of AI's value, cultural buy-in can be elusive. Finally, inadequate training and skill gaps among employees can hinder AI adoption. Without robust upskilling programs, the workforce may struggle to integrate AI tools into daily operations. (ChatGPT, 2024). Based on the scenario presented above, AI requires solid and long-term strategy to deliver an organisational transformation. In the upcoming section, I am presenting an overview of the culture of the banking organisation using the three-levels framework (Stiles, 2024a). Then, in the subsequent sections, I will use the Change Framework (Stiles, 2024b), moving from a current state of conventional retail bank to an improve state of fully enabled AI innovation driven financial institution. III.

Three levels of organisational culture

Below is a summary of the different culture levels related to AI enablement in a banking institution. Artifacts and Espoused values are based on what I did experience in the bank, while Underlying Assumptions is derived from literature review. Artifacts – Based on my experience, the artifacts in terms of technology and resources used by a conventional bank for AI transformation are: -

Dedicated teams of specialists developing AI tools. Repositories of code containing relevant programming resources. Regular sessions to discuss progress, risks and opportunities around projects. Analytical dashboards and metric based reports showing the technical performance of AI algorithms.

Espoused values – There were several initiatives started by leadership as aspiring goals but not always aligned with actual practices: -

C-Level stakeholders stating generic strategies for embracing AI innovation. Measuring customer satisfaction strategies, based on specific goals provided by senior leadership. Guidelines from the Financial Conduct Authority for ethical usage of AI.

15

-

Risk management policies around AI management, how to measure value derived from AI algorithms (subject to vague definitions of value attribution).

Basic underlying assumptions – The hardest to change, given these were defining the persistent organisational behaviour: -

-

IV.

The real DNA of the bank with a unionised workforce, would decelerate sudden changes in work culture. Employees had the perception that most digital transformation efforts were mainly branding. Leaders at banking organisations are good apply the Law 45 of Power "Preach the need for change, but never reform too much at once" (Greene, 1998). There is already a perception about losing jobs to AI due to the massive closure of branches and customer service centres. Job pessimists argue that there would be less jobs than those generated by AI (Tegmark, 2017). People running operations consider having a better view of the real needs of the business, hence they take c-leadership views as aspirational rather than directional (Edmondson, 2011).

Creating a shared need

In the next sections the Change Framework is applied. According to the context introduced before, a shared need for the banking institution can be summarised as thriving in a highly competitive and disruptive market. To do so, innovation and intensive progress through new technologies can position the organisation in a niche for long term success. Digital Innovation needs to be understood by C level stakeholders as "creative destruction". Organisations such as Intel and Reuters, have stopped asking "who else is doing it?" and embrace the long-term rewards worth the risks (Russell-Walling). Intensive progress means doing entirely new things instead of copying competitors (Thiel and Masters, 2024).

V.

Shaping a vision

To avoid been reduced to back-end organisations, key decision makers need to articulate a clear vision. It must deal with the pressures made by regulatory bodies to share data and bring new services. For instance, my institution started embracing new regulation initiatives such as Open Banking (data sharing protocols with other organisations) and it led to new services to their customers. Another organisation, Deustche Bank, has embraced Open Banking to innovate payment services for Business-to-Business customers in Poland (Chishti and Puschmann, 2020).

16

The vision needs to be articulated into a solid and concise aspiration. Organisations leveraging new technologies to multiply their efficiency by a tenfold increase, are defining Massive-Transformative-Purposes MTPs (Ismail, Malon and Van-Geest, 2014). These are aspirational statements that unify transformational needs, inspire employees, retain talent and attract customers. Applied to a commercial bank using AI, could be something as "We will provide the best customised digital journey to customers and offered them an experience second to none". VI.

Mobilising Commitment

To mobilise commitment clear problem definition and objectives need to be disseminated across the whole organisation. Management Consulting experts state that a problem that is well defined is half-solved (Garrette, Phelps and Sibony, 2018). This leads a bank to evaluate where exactly to use AI and deliver the best possible value. In terms of making objectives public across the organisation, Google has been a great example, as there is strong sense of commitment to achieve individual and team goals (Schmidt and Rosenberg, 2014). Navy SEALs lead commitment by prioritising and executing laser focused plans, too much complexity prevents clarity of thought and effectiveness (Willink and Babin, 2015). Complementary skills are equally important for commitment. Employee engagement can be maximised through a culture of experimentation and failure, but with "no tolerance for incompetence" (Pisano, 2019). Political Intelligence, while becoming a trusted advisor and negotiating other managers agendas (Owen,2018), reduces the friction for introducing AI developments across a political organisation as a bank. VII.

Monitoring Progress

From a strategic perspective, understanding all the features and risks from the "terrain" is essential to monitor the transition state of the organisation. A skilled leader adapts to the terrain rather than forcing a rigid plan (Sun Tzu, 1963). This strategic principle applies to AI transformations, since the cultural and organisational terrain can be very challenging to navigate. As discussed in the three-level framework section, it is required to understand each layer of this terrain to ensure that progress is consistent. Measuring what matters through Objectives and Key Results (OKRs) has been the formula of success for several global tech organisations such as Google and originated with Intel's leadership under Andy Grove (Doerr, 2018). The Objective for a bank can be to increase their revenue by 10% annually by using AI, the Key Results to achieve can be in the form of measurable outcomes as high percentage of customers using digital services; high net promoter scores using AI services, etc.

17

VIII.

Making Change Last

As per my days leading AI transformation, a centralised body directing the changes was critical to have long-lasting effects. For instance, AI Council providing guidance at organisational level empowering all parties with the know-how and expertise to have a unified plan (Chishti et al., 2020) ensuring that employees, shareholders and customers fully understand the benefits of AI. Moreover, adequate training with realistic goals and adequate tools is critical for employee engagement. Complex organisations as banks need to be optimised in their hierarchical structures, to disseminate effectively the information and empowering all individuals to be able to do what they need to get things done (Levitin, 2014). This condition usually is not satisfied by most banks, which are regularly described as vertically organised and siloed. Back in those days, another challenge we overcame was ensuring that stakeholders, AI specialists and IT support were working closer together despite the boundaries of departments hierarchies. For C-level leadership, the changes must be impactful and measurable. Effective managers need to match the employee needs with the CEO vision. AI based transformation of a bank can be a lengthy and complex. Such a change needs to align with a narrative of progress and success for the CEO (Bartlett, 2023). Such is the case of Matt Comyn the CEO of Commonwealth Bank of Australia, sharing the success story around GenAI transformation and adoption with solid results on scam reduction and payment processing standards (Weber, 2024). IX. Overall Assessment and Conclusion Addressing the cultural transformation through AI of a banks is complex. Using the Cultural Three-Levels and Change frameworks introduced in the course allow us to bring a solid approach to drive such transformation. Artifacts can be transformed by a flexible approach on long-term success of innovation (Ries, 2011). An open environment to propose new ideas and challenge constructively that strategy has proven meaningful on cultural transformation (Ibarra, Rattan and Johnston, 2018). This enables the right changes on espoused values and underlying assumptions. As per the Change framework, success can be achieved by collaboration between employees, managers and C-Level Stakeholders. Adequate training is essential while investing in continuous education, as I experienced it while leading digital transformation and AI. It is critical as well to have leadership alignment with a solid AI strategy that goes beyond short term goals and tells a success narrative. The right long-term planning and incentives need to be allocated for those leading the efforts of a strategic critical outcome (Groysberg, 2020). Finally, clear communication about benefits of AI and roles impact is vital to overcoming negative assumptions and driving transformation. Managers can get the full support of leadership by articulating clearly how strategic goals are supported by technological development (Ashford, 2015) such as the AI transformation of the financial institution.

18

1. Introduction The present document provides an overview in chronological order of the experience my team and I had over the Cambridge Venture Project (CVP) for our MBA programme. Following instructions the name of the client organisation is not included, and my team members are given different names. Linking the concepts covered during this course in management and the CVP is a great opportunity to put the theory into Praxis (real practice). I take the definition of incident as a particular event during the CVP as an important situation or circumstance that impacted the dynamics of our team while working together, whether could have some friction, confrontation or positive outcomes. There were more than five incidents during the project. The key frameworks applied on the chronological description of the 5 incidents are as follows: • • • • •

Project Funnel Dealing with different personality types Solving conflicts Power management Handling Difficult Conversations

2. Motivation The project funnel introduced during this course (Goodall, 2024a) is a good starting point to define the relevant stages of the project. According to the type of personality tests we had at the beginning of Michaelmas term, I was assessed as balance between driver and analytical (Merril, 1977), this is related to the project funnel framework. As expected through the funnel model, I had to modify my approach towards working with my team as different assumptions were proven to be different in practice. Since an early stage in my career to managed and led multidisciplinary teams, one key constant: "they were economically compensated", with clear HR and work guidelines. However, the CVP was a different experience; yes, there was a client and professionals supporting us to deliver the project, but as discussed in the upcoming sections the motivation on this project varied significantly for each team member. 3. Cambridge Venture Project and Client Context The CVP that my team got assigned had the overall objective of assisting a charitable organisation with an operational question that it would be hard for them to answer by themselves. The client mainly focuses on serving the local community under a relevant humanitarian need, under which different ethnic groups would have specific cultural and ideological views. In a general sense, the scenario presented focused on increasing their overall engagement with their local community, not to increase their revenue but instead focused on serving better their local community as expressed by their CEO.

22

Following the conversations with the client and based on Management Consulting methodologies (Garrette, Phelps and Sibony, 2018), I suggested to define the project using problem tree structures and develop primary and secondary research following that scheme. Primary research was focused on analysing data on reliable public printed material and online. Secondary research focused on conducting interviews with at least 10 professionals in the region with a view on how we could understand and solve the community engagement scenario discussed above. From first impressions on client and team needs, I got a very particular set of assumptions:

I.

II.

Having engaged a worldclass business institution as Cambridge Judge Business School, I understood that the client justification for the project was related to a business need, such as optimising their revenue channels, or donations through their charitable activities. It took us two weeks to validate that this first assumption was not the case, and hence mainly it was driven their need to engage with us from a humanitarian point of view, which in turn prevented the project to have specific quantifiable indicators from a business perspective. Considering the overall reputation of Cambridge University and the branding of Judge Business School, I took the second assumption that the professional and academic calibre of my peer students, would be very high from a commitment and teamwork point of view. As discussed in the upcoming sections there was a high disparity from a motivational angle for the team to take this project. This, based on a fast assessment I had of my team following a renowned framework (Kahneman, 2011). Overall, my purpose was to provide focus, shared leadership and structure for this project.

The task-group-individual needs model (Goodall, 2024b) introduced in the second lecture of this module, addresses how we should have addressed our needs for the CVP. Those needs will be understood while discussing the next incidents and solutions provided.

4. Incidents 4.1 Incident I. Visiting the client site On the second week of having started our CVP, we had an appointment at the client site to discuss further their needs, and the context of their organisation. We got a tour of their facilities, discussed the different charitable activities they run for getting funding, and evaluated potential avenues to assist them. We did not speak that day with the CEO, but with a key projects and communications coordinator.

23

Some of my peers were very quiet up to the point of not asking any question at all, while I was one of the most proactive ones. Nevertheless, it was always my approach to let my peers speak up so they could feel they could participate at any time. The third assumption I had was that the team would have common ground to understand the needs of the customer to increase their community engagement. A second consequence of been a multicultural team was the fact that some of my peers were not familiar at all with that kind of organisation before, since those were not existent in their home countries. The main outcome of this visit was the realisation from everyone in my team about the level of impact the organisation has at individual life level for those community members who need their services. Under such realisation from the team, I had a fourth assumption that they would be very committed to the project, which seemed questionable at the early stages. How to manage multicultural teams was a common topic for both my team and the client site, aiming to increase community engagement from a multicultural perspective. The approach to manage these teams was presented during the course (Brett, 2006).

4.2 Incident II. Big differences on an event perception Following the client visit on the way back, I had a candid but respectful conversation with one of the team members: Ian De. Given her passive style of participation and very limited communication, I asked constructively how did she find the visit and whether she wanted to take a different approach on how it went. Overall, she said that it was a quite interesting place, but she felt very shy to participate. On the other hand, she stated that over the last days she was preparing for a technical job interview as she was so keen to stay in the UK after the MBA. Respectfully, I suggested her, that both for the success of her interviews and for having a more fulfilling experience with the CVP, she needed to speak up more often and not been shy, since that was critical for those outcomes. This was based on a framework to have difficult conversations (Patton, 2019). She appreciated the suggestion stating she need more courage to speak, and asked me for further advice. A few days after, we had our first session of Management Praxis focused on the CVP and team dynamics. One of the key activities was for each team member to express their individual needs about the CVP and their project. Noticing that everyone from both teams in the session spoke except the team member, I kindly ask her to speak so we could understand her needs. This came with the best intention from my end to let her express her needs despite that other members of the two teams were already moving to another topic. So she was losing her chance to speak up.

24

I had an informal chat later that evening with Satyajit, another team member, and he person expressed some concerns that I might have put her "on the spot" and potentially it was a bit shameful for her. I managed to address that with the rest of the team but each member had a different point of view. According to recent research on human memory, our mental agents process differently our memories and previous events (Kahneman, 2011). System 1 (fast thinking) was dominant for our team members who thought she was put on the spot. While System 2 (slow thinking) was dominant for me and Ian De, since both took time to assimilate what happened and she was not offended but appreciated the opportunity to express her needs.

4.3 Incident III. They are not paying us to do this… Despite the cautioning advice of "No asshole behaviour" (Sutton, 2017) at the beginning of this course, there was a negative incident on the second to last week of the project. Satyajit who unfortunately claimed to be the most avid critic of the CVP as a module of the MBA, expressed a shameful statement while been asked to be more involved in the project. Since we could not have our primary research interviews until a very late stage of the project, he kept blaming the client on this slow progress. I stated that it was also our responsibility to check with the client, and provide support or alternatives if they were facing challenges to get the interviews with us confirmed. He replied back, as witnessed by the whole team, stating that he "was not been paid any money for that project" so it was not his problem. In contrast, his main priority during the Michaelmas term was train and dedicate time to his go-kart racing hobby. Later during the evening Ian De confirmed through our chat that she needed to away the next week given a programming Hackaton, so she was happy to help the team over the weekend. Immediately Satyajit, replied (as evidence recorded in our chat) stating that she should not bother as "no-one was paying us to do this …(offensive word omitted)". I spoke with Alice my co-lead of the team and explored avenues to keep high the motivation of the team. By following adaption principles on how to handle "difficult" people (Erikson, 2019), we managed to understand better Satyajit personality. By setting a nonjudgemental environment and facilitating respectful discussions (Toegel, 2016) we managed to have more constructive session with Satyajit. Team conflict was reduced to have a joint session and discuss despite how things were not going as expected, how could we more focus on a final productive week. Acknowledging that Satyajit and Alice had some frictions before, I focused on the impact of previous emotions and ensure we could negotiate a better outcome together (Fisher, 2005).

4.4 Incident IV. Difficult Conversations

25

The framework from Patton to lead difficult conversations (Patton, 2019), led me to take different perspectives on how to take challenging discussions as 1:1's with my team members. The metaphor of "steering the waters" to create momentum (Greene, 1998a), by constructively confronting some of the team members on the previous week led to good outcomes. Satyajit told me at the end of the project, that he did not like to be confronted, as this was a consequence of human nature to be defensive, so he needed to be approached with more empathy (Greene, 2018). Indeed, he appreciated that as an opportunity to prove to the team that he did not want to give an impression of been lazy and focused on getting the interviews done and build the respective reports. During the project there were some relative power struggles with my co-lead Alice. All the way till the end of the CVP she clearly had an impulse to direct the team. There were no intentions from my end to let other team members take ownership of leading. However, her listening and oral skills were significantly limited, to a point that there were contradictory instructions from her end or at least that was the impression of the team. I managed to have two conversations with her addressing constructively that real leaders listen and are not reactive towards what others might think of them. Following the funnel framework, I had two options: a) either minimise efforts, and see how pressure over the team would lead to some outcomes, b) I had to adjust my energy and communication style, and humble down to the needs of the team. Based on a previous Learnings from the corporate world, I focused on the second and use emotional and political intelligence to negotiate a better working scheme. Moreover, I applied Law 7 of Power "Soften People's Resistance by Confirming Their Self-Opinion: The Law of Defensiveness" (Greene, 2018b). Conscious of Alice's interests on applying on Management Consulting roles, I asked her if she thought whether she would face similar power related situations in those roles? She agreed and saw the team dynamics as an opportunity to be better prepared for upcoming interviews and opportunities. The priority for both of us as co-leads was to get the project done and reduce the number of confrontations with our less constructive team member. 4.5 Incident V. Taking Ownership Observing clear lack of structure and motivation from the team, I decided to follow a set of relevant principles stated by an inspiring Navy Seal Jocko Willink (Willink, 2015). Noticing that Steven and Chei Lin were not engaged during different stages of the project, I created project management framework using Trello and Gantt Charts for them to identify how could they contribute better and according to their skills and values so they could be further motivated (Fitzgerald, 2024).

26

Andy Grove, the famous former CEO of Intel, introduced Objectives and Key Results (OKRs) in that company (Tedlow, 2007). He is one of my favourite references on modern management as he transformed Intel into a technology giant. According to Eric Schmidt the former CEO of Google, transparent public communication of aggressive but achievable OKRs, led the organisation to reach great cohesion and effectiveness (Schmidt, 2014). The Nuna Story for OKRs in Health Care (Doerr 2018) is a very inspiring case of team alignment with ambitious objectives in a humanitarian sector. This was related to our CVP and we manged to set similar OKRs for community engagement, outcomes by stakeholders and reaching to critical experts in the field who could help us in our secondary research. Another important contribution from Andy Grove at Intel was conflict resolution based on "Disagree and Commit" (Tedlow, R. 2007). By following his principles on letting everyone express their opinions but also propose a solution, we managed to put our team together. In our team the sense of ownership was accompanied with more freedom to have purpose and autonomy to run the interviews, which in turn led to further engagement with prosocial purpose (Burkus, 2023). We exceeded our OKR of 10 interviews and instead we ran 15 in a record time (less than 7 days). 5. Final presentation Our client became quite satisfied with the work we delivered and in the words of our mentor we got outstanding results, based on the primary and secondary research we delivered. The Client got back to us asking for additional content to share, and appreciated we brought light on how they could better engage with their community by: • • • •

creating joint programmes with health organisations, work with community and ethnic group champions to recommend their services have more inclusive hiring practices, have a more analytical approach to quantify the outcomes of their initiatives.

6. Overall Reflection Learning the right behaviours to know what my team really wanted (Owen, 2018) led me to increase my emotional quotient and discuss my learnings with a leading Professors at Judge Business School and Lecturer of our course. Based on previous sessions it was clearly a dysfunctional team during most of the project as discussed during our CVP focused Management Praxis sessions. We both agree that I did adjust my approach on communicating and leading the team differently. During that session, I referred on how I did adjust to the needs of my team and how I was presenting myself during the joint sessions we have together. By focusing on the behaviour of the team, I adjusted my approach based on selfawareness and asking feedback (Toegel and Barsoux, 2012) from team members and from my Lecturer. Then with the right changes, I increased persuasiveness within a 27

group following "big small changes" (Martin, 2014) on communication and participation. The outcomes we got as a team led to more fulfilling experience at the end of the CVP with stronger motivation and purpose (Kwik, 2020) based on the feedback we got from the client. 7. Conclusion Porter introduced a good approach towards first focusing on one-self to then identify the gaps in the team to manage (Porter, 2019). That led me to change the overall strategy. One of the main situations I had the opportunity to assess about my team, was that we were a multicultural team, and we had different approaches to ask questions. The approach consisted of adapting and using different types of interventions (Brett, Behfar, and Kern, 2006) as summarised in the previous sections. The paradox of excellence (Delong, 2011) is a great way to understand the context of how some of those incidents were perceived by myself as not particularly positive but in the long run, these were opportunities as well. The funnel model allowed me to see the CVP as a learning process to better validate assumptions, test them twice if necessary and focus to deliver according to the needs of my team and how I could contribute better to the team dynamics and pivot towards more productive working schemes (Tamaseb, 2021). Finally, by understanding my needs and my peers' we had an overall better working dynamic. Their needs were to learn at a different pace and make the project as efficient as possible while still making a good contribution. In my case I needed to be a more flexible and understanding team member, consequently, I could fulfil an inner call (Greene, 2012) to be a better leader engaged in humanitarian projects.

MBA117 – Organisations VS Markets

Company: H&M Hennes & Mauritz UK Limited Topic: Emissions/Waste Role: Lending Bank (Lender)

Part 1 – Assessment from a Lending Bank

1.1 Introduction and Motivation This work presents the actionable solution of a lending organisation for a textile manufacturing company aiming to reduce emissions and waste. Working in three financial institutions during my career, has led me to understand the growing pressure from both the markets and regulators towards green lending. Additionally, while working in Management Consulting, I had the opportunity to deliver a project for H&M focused on optimising supply chain transparency, costs and environmental impacts. It was focused on quantifying those metrics and contextualise the intricate dynamics from third party providers. The long-term aspiration was to tokenise textile assets and track them through blockchain (Tapscott, 2016). Based on the previous elements. The upcoming sections will be addressed based on previous professional experience and literature review. 1.2 Bank Lending and Sustainability Guidelines Lending is a complex process where the bank proceeds to provide a loan based on the bargaining position of the business and do an overall risk assessment for defaulting on the debt (Arnold, 2014). The loan agreement is the formal document provided by the lender to determine the terms and conditions, the annual rate, the period to pay it back, late charges and default conditions (DK, 2017). Banks in Europe have been committed to green finance since 2015, and provide more attractive annual rates according to standards of Carbon Emissions reduction (European Investment Bank, 2015). According to the European Parliament and the European Environment Agency, the fashion industry is required to comply with an increasing amount of sustainability regulations (European Parliament, 2024). In March 2022 the European Union launched the Strategy for Sustainable and Circular Textiles. This plan requires textiles to be more durable, reusable and recyclable, reducing the environmental impact of the textile and fashion sectors. Consequently, banks are required to report in detail about the green loans they provide to different businesses (European Banking Authority, 2023). Several Banks in the UK are reporting to both their stakeholders and customers 32

their actions on lending to businesses focused on sustainable development. H&M has delivered several efforts on sustainable development across most of their clothes lines and report the consequent financial and non-financial results (H&M Group, 2023). 1.3 Stakeholders For the purposes of this assessment, stakeholders are defined as per Edward Freeman's 1985 conceptualisation of those individuals or groups that "can affect or are affected" by the organisation activities (Russel-Walling, 2007). This is based on the principle that commercial firms are managed more effectively at strategic level taking the long-term view of those stakeholders. The next subsection presents the primary and secondary stakeholders of the bank relevant to sustainable lending for the Textile Industry. Some of the stakeholders are based definitions of who the main players in corporate finance (Rau, 2017). 1.3.1 Primary Stakeholders Corporate Client – The company applying for corporate loans In this case H&M, which has been introduced previously. Critical individuals to remain in communication with the Bank while addressing the lending requirements are the CEO and the Chief Financial Officer. The CFO creates on an annual basis (regularly) a financial plan that forecasts future needs, identifies funding sources, and determines the strategy to seek loans. Chair and Government Body The Bank's chair and government body is responsible for taking the most important decisions and overseeing the implementation of strategic objectives, including sustainability related loan schemes and approving the corporate culture, amongst others relevant strategic decisions. Bank Shareholders Several global banks including the financial services institution I worked with, had public shares that allow the respective holders to have different levels of partial ownership and influence on the bank decisions. According to their potential voting rights the shareholders can in turn have influence on going ahead with more sustainable lending for the upcoming policies of the bank and its corporate customers. Customers Bank customers concerned of sustainability practices are secondary stakeholders in this situation, since there is a growing awareness of consumers of financial services deciding to do retail banking with their financial institutions based on sustainable principles. For instance, the Corporate Knights ranking provides a good assessment of banks sustainability commitments; it was reported that 2.6 Trillion USD were provided as green finance (Corporate Knights, 2023).

33

1.3.2 Secondary Stakeholders Credit Agencies Credit agencies such as Standard & Poor's (S&P) and Fitch play a major factor ranking the sustainability and green financing of different organisations. In this case both a company such as H&M are ranked on the credit worthiness which in turn has major implications securing new loans and funding. At the same time a lending bank can be ranked on their sustainable lending practices as Fitch Group has introduced the Sustainable Fitch ranking initiative (Fitch Group, 2024). Government Regulators as the FCA and EBA The Financial Conduct Authority and the European Banking Authority are key regulators under which the conditions of lending should be offered to businesses in the UK and EU respectively. Under a new scheme, it has been proposed for European Banks to create a green loan scheme to spur markets and sustainable companies, given the challenges they need to face to be competitive and profitable. (European Banking Authority, 2023b) Not-for-profit climate change organisations Ranking organisations in the topic of sustainability such as the Corporate Knights developing the own methodology to rank top 100 sustainable companies. Also they rank financial institutions (Corporate Knights, 2024). The United Nations as the well renown global organisation has several guidelines for ensuring that global institutions including banks comply with sustainable practices. A relevant guideline is the UN Sustainable Development Goals (United Nations 2024). Both organisations, amongst others, play a major role in the public perception of the bank and H&M too. 1.4 Introduction for the potential conflict Based on the stakeholders introduced previously, there can be a potential conflict of priorities towards the following hypothetical scenario of lending to H&M under green finance principles: "The Bank is considering modifying their lending policies to Textile and Fashion customers as H&M under the grounds that it would be complying with recommendations from the regulators and non-for-profit organisations. This would imply reducing the annual interest rate for those loans and accepting higher likelihood of loan payment default if the borrower was not to be commercially successful". The Primary (PS) and Secondary (SS) Stakeholders are presenting their hypothetical arguments towards the new policy as follows: PS – Bank Governing Body– In favour, it seems to be a good opportunity to improve the long-term relationship with the regulators and government organisations.

34

Conscious of the bad reputation of some competitors (Lawrence, 2018) they would aim to improve the image of the investment bank sector. They have fast assessment based on their experience (Kahneman, 2011) about these sustainable initiatives' success, and achieve favourable conditions from the regulators and government bodies. PS – Corporate Customer– H&M – In Favour, obviously, as they plan to follow the guidelines provided by the European Environment Agency, and the pressure from some of their consumers to move forward with more sustainable practices. Hence, they need the loans from the bank. PS – Shareholders Class A and B– The majority of them is in favour, since they consider this potentially would increase the value of their shares, due to macro trends on the valuation of companies doing low carbon footprint initiatives, and they would vote for approving new policies to lend to those related companies. Shareholders and consumers of financial services are shifting their expectations to get clearer digital insights on long-term performance or organisations (Schatt, 2014). PS – Shareholders Class C– The majority is against since they own their shares for shorter period and don't have voting rights. Nevertheless, they could use other actions to influence other decision makers in the bank. They follow principles on short term investing and mitigating actions to reduce risk (Bogle, 2017). SS – Government Regulators– In Favour, since these regulators plan to increase the spun outs of small companies focused on sustainability. In addition, this would be beneficial to the market. SS – Sustainability Not-for-profit Organisations– In Favour, since they aim for the benefit of the whole community. They are conscious that without proper funding the business models of the sustainable focused companies would not last to make the proper impact. Leadership of the Bank CEO and CFO– Against, lending to this kind of customer seems to be beneficial in the short term only to "green-wash" the image of the bank, but it can lead to higher risk of default. In addition, they have a good understanding of how interconnected markets behave (Easley and Kleinberg, 2018) and see that for the networked pricing dynamics of sustainable clothes and textiles, there are higher risks for unfavourable market conditions. 1.5 Discussion of the Strategy Most of the stakeholders can come under a general agreement to minimise risks of lending to H&M, with an achievable strategy to be completed by 2035. Strategic thinking needs to consider the capabilities of the firm, how they plan to fulfil their customer needs (Owen, 2018) and apply this to their sustainability plan. 1.5.1-Mitigating factors:

35

As the bank representative, I will need to review the borrowing request from H&M CFO. H&M is making a strong commitment to sustainability, requires a detailed analysis and proactive risk management. Below are shown some strategies the bank could implement to minimise the risks associated with this type of loan: •

•

Evaluation of objectives: It is essential to deeply understand H&M's sustainability objectives, key performance indicators (KPIs), and how they align with market trends and environmental regulations. Risk identification: Analyse the risks associated with implementing these initiatives, such as the volatility of sustainable raw material prices, changes in consumer preferences, or competition in this sector. As a bank we will benchmark against other clients that are within the textile sector and do a full financial model of the Weighted Average Cost of Capital as we saw during Corporate Finance session. The Betas of the market, the project and the company will be derived based on the risk-free market rates.

1.5.2- Objectives and Key Results (OKRs): Below are some relevant OKRs (Doerr, 2018) required to be satisfied by 2035: I.

Objective: Ensure comprehensive risk assessment before loan approval a. Key Result: Verify at least 90% accuracy in financial statement evaluations by cross-checking with independent audits. b. Key Result: Ensure that the risky loan undergo stress testing for worstcase scenarios before approval

II.

Objective: Improve monitoring and early warning Systems for the risky loans a. Key Result: Implement real-time monitoring tools that flag any financial distress indicators on H&M financial status (drop in revenue, cash flow issues). b. Key Result: Achieve a minimum Net Interest Margin (NIM) of 5% on highrisk loans.

The measures listed above are examples of what could be done to reduce the risk and get a higher compensation for it. The main alternative to invest onto sustainability committed companies would be renewable energies, which could have a similar environmental impact that textile reduction, but with a lower risk rate. 1.6 Conclusion This first part of the assessment focused on understanding the role it plays a Bank as lender for our textile and fashion company H&M around sustainable lending. Most of the views presented were under the context of how the bank, it's primary and secondary stakeholders would take sides around approving a more sustainable lending policy towards companies as H&M.

36

There are different motivations around going in favour or against the new policy given potential variations on returns with respect to the lending, risk around debt default status and long-term implications for the bank from a Public Relations and profitability perspective. A set of mitigating measures to compensate for a potential higher risk of default, is considered for H&M while requesting a loan for becoming a more sustainable company and reduce waste and pollution at a profitability expense.

Part 2 – Statement and analysis of the other roles perspectives

2.1 Introduction This second part considers the positions of the other team members assuming a specific role as stakeholders or relevant party in this process. Firstly, the most relevant stakeholders from the perspective of the bank are analysed and discussed. Secondly, although not identified as stakeholders, the remaining roles will be evaluated from their arguments. 2.2 Analysis 2.2.1 Government Body As discussed in Part 1. This primary stakeholder is one of the most important ones, since they approve new legislation, financial benefits and the overall government set of initiatives that will play a major role in the success of funding and lending to businesses focused on sustainability. Carbon taxation and carbon credit trading are two relevant concepts introduced, which help to incentivise corporate accountability. As per the previously introduced objectives it would help the bank to rank different customers based on their actual metrics and key quantitative results on waste reduction in the form of OKRs (Doer, 2018). Modular production is a technical approach focused on reducing waste for the textile and fashion sector. 2.2.2 CEO This is one of the most important roles, and as exposed in Part 1, the CEO of H&M should present a solid plan on how their sustainability strategy should be including applying for lending or funding and provide more context on how to reduce waste as a top polluter in their sector. The way the content is presented reflects a superficial assessment of reference material copying and sticking together several pieces of text from other sources unfortunately. Consequently, poor definition of market conditions, stakeholders and limited strategy are shown. Focusing on the meaningful points, the transition to waste reduction operations is costly from a know-how and technical point of view. To overcome this challenge the CEO relies mainly on relying on consumer trends and government support, while loans and investors are not mentioned. Stakeholders as investors and banks would find it challenging to provide a loan to this

37

client under the context mentioned above. It would be beneficial if he could add an structured strategy with clear milestones and objectives to get to 2035 by OKRs (Schmidt, 2014). 2.2.3 Investor There are some elements of similarity with respect to the bank perspective presented in Part 1. There are similarities with respect to reducing risk. While the bank assess risk on an individual basis of the borrower to go into default, the investor focuses on reducing risk from a portfolio diversification perspective. The proposed market-based and firm-based approaches to reduce emissions and waste resonate consistent with what is expected by the bank, the NGO and the government stakeholders. The team member describes in good detail some of the economic challenges and logistics for H&M to run their sustainable initiatives smoothly. There is a good exposure on how limited yet is the recycling of used clothes as a small fraction of all produced and sold clothes. Despite new green funding schemes, it is questioned whether robust monitoring and reporting of the benefits of these programmes do really work. All these facts are presented from a risk assessment perspective. 2.2.4 Not-for-profit organisations This is not a major stakeholder for the bank, as it qualifies as secondary. The team member defining the perspective for that role fall short of understanding who their real stakeholders should be. Such an organisation should be accountable first to society and consumers. The concept of carbon pricing mechanisms the team member suggests, is a potential viable solution that leads to quantify more reliably the carbon footprint for the textile organisation. The comprehensive emissions accounting concept reinforces a previous claim in Part 1, that this would let the bank as lender to fully assess the impact of the initiatives started by H&M, and determine whether there is solid outcomes, based on the lent money, and validate waste reduction and environmental impact 2.2.5 Politician This is a relevant role to discuss public policy making, it would be more valuable to be provided within a European politics perspective instead of American, since the other roles and H&M are based in Europe. There is a very strong bias to analyse the context presented from a U.S perspective instead. The public and private partnering for innovation, seems to be appealing though. There is consistency with the government role for promoting carbon pricing and taxing; likewise, there is overlap position of the NGO while pursuing wider social well-being and partnering with these organisations to educate consumers on sustainable fashion choices. Relevant metrics are mentioned for actual efforts on recycling such as 50% of all materials to be recycled by 2030. Tax credits and regional recycling centres would be beneficial to reduce their cost base, while proving good outcomes on waste

38

reduction. This in turn would reduce the estimated chances of going to default if they were to be provided a loan by the bank as exposed in Part 1.

2.3 Conclusion Based on the cased of H&M scenario in Sustainable Textile Development, perspectives vary significantly across the six stakeholders discussed in the previous sections. The investor role in contrast, seeks market growth and profitability, weighing sustainability against competitive advantage and consumer demand. Similarly, a government body focuses on regulatory compliance, national sustainability goals, and economic impact, ensuring alignment with environmental and trade policies. The notfor-profit organisation, however, emphasised ethical sourcing, environmental responsibility, and fair labour practices, advocating for systemic change over financial returns. The politician should view the investment as a policy lever, balancing economic growth and environmental. Lastly, the company CEO must integrate sustainability with corporate strategy, balancing costs, consumer trends, and regulatory mandates while maintaining profitability. Finally, while stakeholder might value sustainable textile development, their motivations such as: short vs long term profit, impact, or strategy cab shape distinct approaches. The actionable solution presented by the bank I represent prioritises financial outcomes and return, assessing long-term environmental impact and minimise loan default risks through responsible lending and OKRs to fulfil by 2035.

This approach leverages Alpha's stability and proven traction, Beta's high growth potential, and Gamma's moderate valuation with scaling potential. Investing £60,000 in Alpha ensures exposure to a well-established company with global industry partnerships and strong government backing, while minimizing dilution risk. Although Alpha's valuation is higher, it offers long-term stability and lower downside risk compared to the other two companies as a relatively matured company. Increasing the investment in Beta to £50,000 takes advantage of its lower pre-money valuation, offering a larger ownership stake and higher potential upside. However, Beta carries a higher dilution risk due to its funding needs, meaning future rounds could impact investor returns. Keeping £40,000 in Gamma provides moderate exposure to a company with solid growth prospects, while acknowledging its significant dilution risk. With a wellbalanced allocation, this strategy allows for both high-return opportunities and downside protection, making it an optimal mix for a diversified investment portfolio.
