Introduction

This work summarises an assessment towards how retail mutual funds managers can evaluate the impact of investing in polluting and not polluting US stock firms. In consistency with other courses of the MBA, it is clear the financial sector has increasingly recognised the importance of sustainability, with pollution emerging as a key consideration in investment decisions. The United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly Goal 13 (Climate Action) and Goal 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production), emphasise the need for businesses to reduce their environmental impact (United Nations, 2024). As it is the cases in UK, USA and Europe, their governments are introducing stricter regulations and investors shift towards Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) investing. As it is stated along this assessment, pollution can be considered both a risk factor and a behavioural factor affecting stock performance. For retail mutual funds as per the simulated PMC scenario of the assignment, this dual perspective is crucial. In general, high-pollution (P) firms may offer higher returns but face greater regulatory and transition risks, aligning with SDG-driven policies that discourage unsustainable practices. In contrast, low-pollution firms (C) may benefit from the increasing preference for ESG investments but risk overvaluation due to excessive demand. Understanding how pollution influences asset pricing can help retail mutual funds better deal with these complexities while contributing to global sustainability efforts. By the end of the discussion, a formal statement is presented on whether pollution is found to be a risk or a behavioural factor.

Discussion Regulations and rankings Over more recent years, sustainable investing seems to align with global initiatives like the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). This is mean to address concerns about the cost of sustainability. According to leading financial publication firms that prioritise sustainability often face higher operational costs, such as investing in cleaner technologies, complying with stricter regulations, and meeting ESG reporting requirements (The Economist, 2018). The Corporate Knights ranking provides investors with a transparent evaluation of the world's most sustainable companies, helping them align investments with Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) criteria. By analysing key sustainability metrics such as carbon emissions, resource efficiency, and ethical governance, the ranking aids in identifying firms with long-term growth potential and lower regulatory risks (Corporate Knights, 2024). This supports informed, responsible investment decisions.

56

US Stocks and pollution scrutiny Stocks of US firms are increasingly subject to higher levels of pollution scrutiny, particularly from mutual funds that integrate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) criteria into their investment strategies. Regulatory bodies, such as the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), have introduced enhanced climaterelated disclosure requirements, compelling publicly traded companies to report their carbon emissions and sustainability risks (SEC, 2022, pp. 15-18). Additionally, institutional investors and mutual funds are aligning their portfolios with sustainability goals, applying stricter screening measures to exclude or underweight high-pollution firms. This shift is driven by the growing financial risks associated with environmental non-compliance, including potential litigation, carbon taxation, and reputational damage, which can negatively impact stock valuations and investor confidence. Furthermore, the rise of sustainable investment indices and corporate ranking systems, such as the Corporate Knights Global 100, previously introduced, has intensified scrutiny on US firms' pollution levels. Mutual funds managing ESG-focused portfolios must consider how firms comply with evolving environmental regulations and consumer expectations regarding sustainability (Corporate Knights, 2024). Firms with weak pollution controls face divestment risks as ESG-driven capital shifts towards lower-carbon companies. This increased scrutiny affects asset pricing and sectoral capital flows, reinforcing the need for mutual funds to incorporate pollution risk assessments into their investment strategies. Mutual funds, risks and behavioural factors Mutual funds collect capital from multiple investors to create a diversified portfolio of assets, managed by professional fund managers. Diversification helps reduce unsystematic risk while asset allocation strategies manage exposure to broader market risks (Reilly and Brown, 2021). To handle risk factors, such as economic downturns or regulatory changes, mutual funds use portfolio diversification, hedging techniques, and sector rotation (Elton et al., 2020). Behavioural factors, such as investor biases and market sentiment, are addressed by mutual funds through investment strategies, contrarian approaches, and ESG integration to avoid mispricing and overvaluation. By balancing these factors, mutual funds aim to achieve consistent, risk-adjusted returns (Barberis and Thales, 2003). These techniques can be relevant for the current focus on whether it is possible to optimise the performance of the investment portfolio presented for the polluting and non-polluting firms. Applicability on retail mutual funds For a retail mutual fund, the scenario presented for Clean vs Polluting firms, creates a trade-off between ethical investing and financial returns. High-pollution firms may offer higher expected returns as compensation for regulatory and transition risks, while lowpollution firms may be benefited by a green premium, leading to overvaluation and 57

lower future returns. The mutual fund must balance sustainability goals with financial performance, with consideration on assessing whether the cost of sustainability really leads to potential long-term benefits. This makes clear the need for strategic asset allocation integrating risk-adjusted returns and ESG considerations, ensuring longterm profitability without compromising environmental responsibility. Pollution related factors Pollution is considered as a risk factor when it is linked to risk exposure, as investors demand higher returns for holding stocks of firms exposed to regulatory costs, climate risks, and transition risks (Engle et al., 2020, pp. 45-48). Stricter environmental policies and carbon pricing increase operational costs for high-emission firms, affecting profitability and market valuation (Ilhan, Sautner and Vilkov, 2021, pp. 320-323). These financial risks contribute to the higher expected returns of polluting firms. This in turn reflects the market's compensation for heightened uncertainty. This assessment aligns with identifying pollution mainly as a risk factor rather than behavioural factor. This is based on the previous statements on the regulatory ecosystem initiated by the UN Sustainable Development Goals, Corporate Knights Rankings and the higher returns expected by investors. A key approach to mitigating this risk factor in retail mutual fund strategies is the use of an established factor model in investment decision-making. By incorporating recognised factor modelling techniques, mutual funds can better assess and compensate for risk exposure, enhancing portfolio diversification and return optimisation (Fama, E. F. and French, 2015). Fama-French factor modelling Incorporating environmental factor modelling into investment strategies is essential for mutual funds aiming to achieve long-term, risk-adjusted returns. Sustainability concerns are increasingly influencing asset pricing, making it crucial for funds to integrate ESG considerations into their portfolio construction. A key approach involves tilting investments towards low-carbon firms while maintaining sufficient diversification to avoid overvaluation. Factor-based models that account for environmental risks allow mutual funds to balance return potential with sustainability objectives (Ilmanen, 2022). By integrating environmental factor modelling, the retail mutual fund can effectively navigate market uncertainties while aligning with long-term sustainability trends. The Fama-French three-factor model is relevant for risk factors in mutual fund investments, as it explains asset returns based on market risk, size, and value factors (Fama and French, 1993, pp. 5-8). This approach assumes that investors require compensation for systematic risks rather than being driven by behavioural biases. While behavioural factors can influence short-term pricing inefficiencies. This model aligns with risk-based explanations of stock returns, guiding mutual funds in constructing diversified portfolios to optimise risk-adjusted performance (Bodie, Kane and Marcus, 2021, pp. 334-338).

58

Conclusion This assessment has explored the dual perspective of pollution as both a risk factor and a behavioural factor in the context of retail mutual fund investments. Through an analysis of regulatory frameworks, sustainability rankings, and financial modelling techniques, it has been demonstrated that pollution aligns more closely with a riskbased perspective, specially around stocks of US firms. Stricter environmental policies, carbon pricing, and transition risks create financial uncertainties for polluting firms, necessitating higher expected returns to compensate for these risks. The Corporate Knights ranking and the UN Sustainable Development Goals reinforce the increasing importance of sustainability in investment decisions, further shaping market expectations and asset pricing. For a retail mutual fund, balancing financial performance with sustainability considerations remains a key challenge. The trade-off between investing in highpollution (P) firms with higher returns and low-pollution (C) firms with potential overvaluation justifies the need for strategic asset allocation. The integration of factor modelling, such as the Fama-French approach, provides a structured method to assess and manage risk-adjusted returns while aligning with evolving ESG considerations. As the financial sector has increasing influence from regulatory and investor-driven sustainability trends, the retail mutual fund must employ comprehensive risk management strategies to navigate the complexities of pollutionrelated investment decisions while maintaining long-term profitability and environmental responsibility.

1. Introduction and motivation This work is focused on the ethical, social, and governance context of one of the most influential Technology organisations over the last 20 years. Enabled by a well sustained leadership in the social media landscape, Meta Platforms Inc. (previously known as Facebook Inc.) leads the race on highly influential digital channels: Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram. By the time of the writing of this assessment, Meta had been on the news very recently based on the controversial decision of laying off several employees across their global operations, and simultaneously, increase significantly the compensation packages of the executive leadership board (Business Insider, 2025). A similar restructuring context occurred in 2023 (Sorkin, 2023); conversely, back then this led to overall long-term good financial performance as expected by the decision makers. While these decisions might be controversial, their argument is to provide long lasting corporate and tech leadership, as it has been the case for similar technology organisations (ABC News, 2024). Motivation A key driver of my career is network-based representations, which model complex systems in social, financial, and economic contexts. Meta innovates on these areas, not just as a digital platform but as a powerful network shaping influence, marketing, and public opinion, rapidly transforming societal, political, and economic dynamics. Following the instructions of the assessment, it will be covered the organisation's board leadership structure and ownership; its compensation structure and situation; the general context in which it operates; relevant social and ethical issues derived from its policies of AI; internal control systems and relationships with stakeholders. Structure of this assessment The structure of this work is as follows: Firstly, the discussion examines Meta's leadership, corporate governance, and financial compensation policies, assessing their alignment with ethical and strategic objectives. Secondly, it evaluates employee relations, focusing on structural changes, talent disruption, and retention strategies to ensure workforce stability despite layoffs. Thirdly, the document explores stakeholder engagement, highlighting communication, transparency, and ethical considerations related to AI governance and misinformation. Subsequently, the analysis addresses corporate governance controls, distinguishing between internal mechanisms—such as board oversight, audits, and risk management—and external controls, including shareholder activism, regulation, and independent audits. Lastly, the conclusion outlines recommendations for ensuring long-term credibility and success for all parties, reinforcing Meta's mission. In the upcoming sections, the Corporate Governance and Ethics course will be referred as "the course", Meta Platforms, Inc. will be referred as Meta. Relevant online sources material is referred following Harvard Style (Pears, R. and Shields, 2022).

62

2. Discussion Meta Platforms, Inc. has been one of the world's most influential technology companies, covering social media, artificial intelligence, and virtual reality. However, its leadership, ethical practices, and corporate governance have faced intense scrutiny. The company's executive compensation, workforce management, and sustainability efforts have raised critical concerns regarding ethical decision-making and governance, specially reflected in recent news as mentioned in the introduction. The following sections discuss Meta's corporate leadership, financial compensation, ethical considerations on AI, governance structure, and sustainability commitments. 2.1

Board Leadership and Compensation

Meta's governance structure is highly centralised since it was originally created as a startup with strong Founder's ownership. Mark Zuckerberg the main founder, retains significant control through dual-class shares according to Kirkpatrick (2010, p. 215). Dual-class shares as introduced during the course (Learmount & Stiles, 2025b) have characterised highly successful Tech IPOS offering about 10x of the voting rights than public Class A shares. Hence, it gives significant control to the main founder. Unlike companies with more independent board oversight, Meta's founder-centric leadership seems to be limiting accountability as suggested by Galloway (2020, p. 127). This model aligns with the assertion from Greene (1998, p. 54) that power consolidation can both protect and hinder a leader's long-term influence. Meta's Board of Directors includes figures from technology and business sectors, with relatively less shares ownership than other technology companies due to the shares distribution mentioned previously. It is reported that governance issues persist, particularly regarding executive remuneration policies according to Lazonick, (2014, p. 33). The Compensation, Nominating, and Governance Committee (CNGC) recently approved substantial executive bonuses despite declining employee job security (SFGate, 2025). More specifically, it approved executive bonuses up to 200% of salaries while simultaneously conducting mass layoffs. This raises concerns about corporate fairness, as job cuts affect lower-level employees while executives receive increased financial incentives. Consequently, Meta's leadership and stakeholders should communicate how these measures will translate into specific results over 2025. As discussed in the first unit of the course, excessive compensation for company executives might lead to potential long-term risks (Learmount & Stiles, 2025a). These decisions have been criticised for prioritising short-term stock performance over longterm employee stability as summarised by Lipton & Rosenblum (2022, pp. 22-37). Doerr (2018, p. 76) argues that aligning executive compensation with long-term objectives, as outlined in OKRs (Objectives and Key Results), could mitigate such governance challenges. In this case the OKRs for the Board of Directors could be related towards financial outcomes, stakeholder engagement and consistent

63

behaviour with Meta's mission: "to give people the power to build community and bring the world closer together" (Meta, 2021). 2.2 Employee Relations Structural changes Meta's handling of employee relations has been controversial, with mass layoffs over previous years. This according to Bail (2021, pp. 47-62) challenges its commitments to workforce development. Reports indicate how employees might perceive these actions, particularly considering restructuring efforts focused on reducing operational costs (NYPost, 2025). This reflects the importance of learning from organisational failure, as outlined by Edmondson (2011, p. 5), who emphasises the need for leadership to foster a learning culture rather than one of job instability. Talent Disruption Talent disruption remains a challenge for Meta, as its rapid technological advancements create internal disruptions. Groysberg, Bhogal, and Mathews (2020, p. 86) argue that firms must assess whether retaining top talent is worth the effort or if new leadership can drive innovation. Moreover, Maxwell (2007, p. 22) stresses that talent alone is insufficient; a supportive corporate culture is essential for sustainable success. Stakeholder capitalism, as covered in the course (Learmount & Stiles, 2025d), could play a critical role in shifting corporate focus from short-term profitability to long-term stakeholder engagement. Talent retention Based on the provided context, it is crucial for Meta to implement strategies that support and engage remaining employees. Providing opportunities for employees to learn new technology and upskill themselves through training and development programmes can enhance their sense of value and commitment to the organisation. Creating an environment that encourages open communication, and the sharing of ideas further fosters engagement and loyalty (Advanced, 2024). Additionally, offering support for employee health and wellbeing plays a crucial role in retention strategies, as employees are more likely to remain with an organisation that demonstrates genuine concern for their overall welfare (HR News, 2024). By investing in employee development and well-being, Meta can maintain a motivated workforce, this can work posterior to the commented workforce reductions. 2.3 Stakeholder engagement To address corporate fairness stakeholder engagement for Meta is critical. The focus of this section is the job cuts can affect lower-level employees while executives receive increased financial incentives. Bartlett (2023, p. 163) underscores that effective leadership requires balancing financial incentives with ethical responsibility. 64

Communication with stakeholders To enhance stakeholder engagement without resorting to controversial business decisions, Meta can adopt a comprehensive communication strategy that emphasises transparency and inclusivity. Developing a well-defined communication plan is essential for effective stakeholder engagement, since it conveys the goals of communication efforts, identifies target audiences, specifies the channels and methods to be used, and sets a timeline for implementation. Tailoring this plan to the specific needs and expectations of stakeholders ensures that communication is both relevant and effective (Askel Sustainability Solutions, 2024). Openness and feedback By proactively addressing stakeholder concerns and fostering open dialogues, Meta can build trust and strengthen its reputation, consequently mitigating potential conflicts and aligning business practices with stakeholder expectations. The governance model of Meta incorporates stakeholder feedback, particularly regarding AI ethics and misinformation management. Through partnerships with external fact auditors, the company ensures that AI-generated content aligns with public interest and community standards (Meta, 2024).

2.4 Social and Ethical Issues derived from Data and AI This section comments on relevant challenges on the usage of Data and AI as reported by different sources, considering key implications for users and their communities. Privacy and inclusion A relevant major ethical concern is data privacy and user manipulation. Meta has been involved in several scandals, most notably the Cambridge Analytica data breach, where user data was used for political advertising without consent as discussed by Zuboff (2019, p. 211). Previous research indicates that algorithmic decision-making can reinforce systemic biases and contribute to the marginalisation of certain communities as argued by Benjamin (2019, p. 41). Regarding this matter, one of the most relevant cases is the impact of news feed algorithms reflecting what most of the users consume which in turn might neglect the needs of minority groups. Content Moderation Meta's implementation of generative AI (GenAI) raises significant strategic and ethical concerns. It also brings additional concerns on AI-driven content moderation and its implications on bias, surveillance, and ethical AI deployment (Noble, 2018, p. 120). Pisano (2019, p. 12) similarly, states that while innovative cultures embrace risk, they must also establish robust mechanisms to mitigate ethical lapses. Tegmark (2017, p. 65

154) warns that AI's rapid progression could leave behind ethical safeguards, leading to unintended societal consequences. Consequently, this might lead to society facing new challenges since AI moves faster than other entities capable of regulating it. Furthermore, content moderation and misinformation remain persistent ethical challenges. The company's reliance on artificial intelligence for moderation has been considered limited on reducing the spread of harmful content (Gillespie, 2018, p. 66). This a relevant topic considering recent changes in content moderation since January 2025 due to major shifts in politics and government agendas. Next are described some relevant frameworks and schemes to counteract the AI challenges at organisational level. 2.5 Ethical Frameworks The course presented relevant frameworks on ethics, specifically towards authenticity and normative approaches (Learmount & Stiles, 2025c). Ismail, Malone, and VanGeest (2014, p. 98) sustain that exponential organisations (as Meta) must adopt ethical AI frameworks to ensure technological growth does not come at the cost of social equity. Next, are the frameworks and relevant actions that Meta has committed to address. Authenticity Framework Tapscott and Williams (2006, p. 73) highlight that transparency and user trust are key to digital corporate success, an area where Meta continues to face challenges. Russell-Walling (2007, p. 102) suggests that proactive corporate ethics, rather than reactive responses to crises, are essential in maintaining public trust. To counteract these risks, Meta focuses through an authentic approach on educating users, implementing stronger AI detection mechanisms (Meta, 2024). By applying the learnings of the course, it would be expected from stakeholders' point of view to keep track of both the news and responses from Meta towards measuring the authenticity of the respective outcomes to then drive constructive conversations with senior leadership. Normative Framework This framework is based on how an organisation like Meta can follow guidelines and standards rooted fairness, legislation and accountability. For instance, best practices in AI governance recommend independent oversight mechanisms to ensure compliance with ethical data use as presented by Cihon, Schuett and Baum (2021, p. 17). Meta acknowledges the risks associated with AI-generated content and misinformation (Meta, 2024) hence it has defined new normative internal approaches to track reduction on misinformation and collaborating with policymakers (Meta 2024). In this context, managers at Meta should be further empowered with well-defined guidelines to take ethical decisions aiming to keep the best interests of the users and their respective communities.

66

Behavioural Framework This framework is focused on how Meta could take critical decisions based the psychology and behaviour of their users. For instance, to improve its GenAI strategy, Meta should align its AI initiatives with ethical guidelines that prioritise user benefits and behaviour, as suggested by Clark (2023, p. 76). Clark highlights that AI can be used to support learning and development when designed with inclusivity in mind. By enhancing AI literacy among users and employees, Meta can build trust and enable responsible AI deployment. Additionally, Marr (2024, p. 112) suggests that AI applications should focus on social good, such as improving access to education, healthcare, and online safety, rather than solely maximising engagement and profit. Cihon, Schuett, and Baum (2021, p. 12) recommend that AI governance structures within corporations incorporate multi-stakeholder perspectives from behavioural factors to ensure AI development aligns with public interest. 2.6 Defining Corporate Governance Controls As covered during the course, firms with strong governance frameworks (Learmount & Stiles, 2025d) are better equipped to manage workforce relations and mitigate reputational risks associated with layoffs. Based on those frameworks Meta can reconcile the recent compensation and layoff actions with its mission stated earlier in this work. The technology giant can enhance its credibility through both internal and external controls: Internal Controls a) Board of Directors: The board should ensure that executive compensation aligns with long-term company performance and stakeholder interests. Implementing performance metrics tied to community-building digital initiatives can demonstrate commitment to Meta's mission. b) Internal Audit: Conducting regular audits to assess the impact of layoffs on remaining employees and overall company culture can provide insights into maintaining a supportive environment, essential for fostering community within the organisation. For instance, measure how new AI tools increase efficiency for writing, testing and deploying new code for developers (Winbuzzer, 2024). c) Executive Compensation: If executive bonuses have increased to 200%, these need to be linked to the overall wellbeing of the organisation and the ecosystem it serves. Full ownership of the outcomes end to end is critical for overall strategic success as demonstrated by Willink and Babin (2015, pp. 166-168). It is required to own and deliver on metrics such as employee satisfaction, community engagement, AI ethical enablement and social impact. This implies full alignment of leadership incentives with the Meta's mission previously stated.

67

d) Risk/Compliance: Establishing robust compliance programs to monitor and mitigate risks associated with workforce reductions and public perception can help maintain trust among stakeholders. External Controls: a) Shareholder Activism: Engaging with shareholders who advocate for equitable compensation practices and ethical governance can pressure Meta to align its actions with its stated social and community integration commitments. b) Regulation: Adhering to labour laws and regulations ensures fair treatment of employees, reinforcing the company's commitment to building a positive community. c) Media: Transparent communication with media outlets about the rationale behind compensation and layoff decisions can help manage public perception and demonstrate accountability. d) External Audit: Engaging independent auditors to review and report on the company's compensation practices and their alignment with corporate values can provide objective assessments to stakeholders (The Institute of Internal Auditors, 2009). By implementing the controls mentioned above, Meta can work towards aligning its internal practices with its mission. This will enhance credibility and fostering a culture that truly empowers users, managers, stakeholders and communities. 2.7 Enabling transparent and effective governance To strengthen its corporate governance and ensure long-term sustainability, Meta could adopt a more inclusive and transparent governance framework. This can be achieved through greater board independence, enhanced stakeholder engagement, and sustainable business practices as presented next. I.

II.

III.

Firstly, board independence is crucial for corporate accountability. Lipton, Cain, and Rosenblum (2023, p. 8) state that effective governance requires active risk oversight, particularly concerning AI governance and ethical decision-making. Meta could, for instance, hire independent directors with expertise in digital ethics, AI governance, and sustainability to balance executive influence. Secondly, stakeholder engagement must be prioritised. As covered during the course, the growing importance of stakeholder capitalism needs to be addressed since corporations consider the long-term interests of employees, customers, and communities (Learmount and Stiles, 2025d). Meta can improve its governance by increasing transparency in decision-making and incorporating stakeholder input into corporate strategies. Lastly, sustainable business practices should be deeply integrated into Meta's operational model. Cihon, Schuett, and Baum (2021, p. 12) suggest that AI corporations should establish multi-stakeholder governance structures to 68

ensure responsible AI deployment and long-term social benefits. Meta must go beyond regulatory compliance and implement stringent ethical AI standards that align with sustainability goals. By acting on these measures, Meta can strengthen its corporate governance framework, mitigate reputational risks, and ensure long-term sustainability while fostering stakeholder trust. Owen (2018, p. 145) emphasises that genuine corporate responsibility requires consistent, measurable progress rather than superficial aspirations. Hence, the actions presented above could be tracked with clear Objectives and Key Results to be presented to both stakeholders, users and employees.

3. Conclusion Meta leads social networks around the world through their innovation; however, recent executive compensation increases, and workforce reductions have raised ethical and governance concerns. Its executive compensation policies highlight a disconnect between corporate leadership and employee welfare, raising concerns about governance effectiveness. This work has explored Meta's corporate governance structure, analysing its board leadership, financial compensation policies, and ethical implications of AI deployment. Considering its leadership in technology, and to maintain its credibility and alignment with its mission, Meta must implement robust governance frameworks. These frameworks on governance, ethics and stakeholder engagement were introduced during the course and discussed in this assessment. Enhancing board independence, internal audits, and executive compensation alignment with long-term objectives will reinforce ethical leadership. Strengthening stakeholder engagement, ensuring transparent communication, and following to ethical AI principles are crucial in addressing scrutiny from the stakeholders, user and wider community. Furthermore, adopting sustainable business practices and ensuring regulatory compliance will safeguard Meta's long-term corporate integrity and reputation. While AI presents new ethical challenges, proactive governance and ethical AI frameworks can mitigate risks. By fostering transparency, accountability, and inclusivity, Meta can balance innovation with responsibility, ensuring sustainable growth and community trust. Overall, Meta must enhance corporate accountability, ethical leadership, and consistent business practices to maintain credibility and stakeholder trust. Hence, a transparent governance structure, ethical leadership, and meaningful stakeholder engagement will be pivotal for Meta to sustain its competitive edge while embracing its mission to connect communities and build a more inclusive digital world.

1. Introduction This assessment is focused on implementing relevant strategic frameworks on the presented strategies during the final session of the Strategy course. The AI Wars case study (Wu et al., 2022) discussed in a previous session of the course, defined the background context for this assessment. It explored the evolving competition in generative artificial intelligence commercialisation and development, focusing on major industry players including Meta. In accordance with the assignment instructions to select a company from those presented in the final session of the course, Meta has been chosen for this task. Some of the key motivators for this selection were: a) its large established user base as a global social networking platform, b) a clear disruptive proposition on open-weight Large Language Models (LLMs) development and c) major AI plans for widespread implementation of AI into their platforms (Business Insider, 2025). The presented overarching strategy for Meta presented by study group 40 (Study Group 40, 2024), will be referred to as Strategy-40. All reference sources are cited using Harvard referencing (Pears and Shields, 2022). The Discussion section introduces this strategy and challenges it under relevant frameworks presented during the course. 2. Discussion 2.1 Overview of Strategy-40 Meta's AI strategy is focused on consolidating its dominance in social media engagement, platform expansion and personalised digital advertisement. By investing $65 billion in AI infrastructure in 2025, the company aims to take leadership in generative AI, particularly with its open-source Llama models. The Strategy-40 goes in alignment with these statements, specifically it provides an overview to execute a $165 billion investment plan (Study Group 40, 2025) focusing on the following principles: •

• • •

Investing $65 billion in AI infrastructure, leveraging Llama, its open-source generative AI model improving ad personalisation, content delivery and platform engagement. Commoditise GenAI models while developing specialist AI tools for advertising and content creation. Future expansion includes integrating new platforms (AR/VR, shopping, search, assistants) and potential joint ventures or acquisitions. Get the funding by relying on cash reserves, debt financing, and asset sales.

74

A core aspect of the strategy involves a unique approach on generalist AI models focused on open-weight framework (the weights of the models are publicly available) and this represents a major difference compared to the GenAI approach compared to Meta's competitors. The models are trained with proprietary data AI for advertising, content creation, and recommendation algorithms. These are the most relevant venues from GenAI to generate impact in societies and business ecosystems according to Marr (2024, pp. 29-32). Assessment of the presented strategy Following the assessment's instructions, the upcoming analysis applies two critical frameworks—VRIO and Network Effects—to evaluate the Strategy-40 as presented by their team. These frameworks are particularly relevant. To be as specific and illustrative as possible with the content provided by them, some of the graphs and slides from their presentation are included in the discussion below. Following the frameworks an overall assessment of the strategy according to Rumelt (2011, pp. 7781) is presented at the end of this discussion section. 2.2 VRIO Framework The VRIO (Value, Rarity, Imitability, Organisation) framework developed by Barney (Barney, 1991) and was discussed in the course by (Coleridge, 2025a). It can be used to evaluate Meta's AI-driven competitive advantage. This framework is applied to Strategy-40 addressing strengths and areas of opportunity. Value Strategy-40 refers to "Meta as a Merchant for Human Attention". This seems to be a over-simplifying definition given their impact on global connectivity and Meta's mission: "to give people the power to build community and bring the world closer together" (Meta, 2021). Meta's capabilities on AI also add value on content licensing agreements, business solutions, reality labs and business messaging services (Meta, 2025). For this assessment the value generation is focused on GenAI. Strength - Larger Language Model Meta AI or "Llama", claims to add value by democratising AI access and enhancing personalised content recommendations (Meta, 2024b). This is reflected in Strategy-40 and Meta has done it early following its inception. The strategy aligns with Thiel and Masters' (2014) insight on how firstmovers in AI can secure lasting value. Their platform monetises human attention through AI-driven recommendations increasing customer retention and engagement. Additionally, efficient ad personalisation and targeting generates value for advertisers.

75

As articulated in The AI Book, companies leveraging AI-driven platforms must manage not only technical challenges but also regulatory scrutiny and ethical implications (Chishti et al., 2020, pp. 26-27). While AI models can be replicated, Meta's deep integration within its digital ecosystem makes imitation difficult at scale (Meta, 2021). Collect and process vast user data sets provides personalised ad targeting schemes that competitors cannot easily match. Synthetic data and continuous AI training designs create further barriers to imitation. Complexity through instantaneous targeted content. This operational structure, in turns should align with Lean Startup methodologies, ensuring AI investments align with real-time user engagement data (Ries, 2011, pp. 260-265).

Weaknesses: • •

2.4 Overall Assessment Meta demonstrates moderate strength in VRIO and network effects but has critical weaknesses. It excels in value creation through AI-driven personalisation and data analytics but lacks clarity in regulatory execution and retention strategies. Network effects remain strong, with 3.4 billion users reinforcing direct and indirect engagement, yet gaps in AI infrastructure investment details and ecosystem expansion plans weaken long-term positioning. Strategic alignment in AI commoditisation is promising, yet competitor adaptability (e.g., DeepSeek, Google) challenges uniqueness. Regulatory foresight is superficial, potentially limiting scalability. Addressing execution gaps in AI integration, compliance, and infrastructure expansion is crucial for maintaining dominance in a rapidly evolving AI landscape. Conclusion According to Rumelt (2011, pp. 77-81), a Good Strategy has: clear diagnosis, guiding policies, coherent actions, competitive advantages and adaptability. Whereas a Bad Strategy presents: vague statements; failure to identify the problem; conflicting goals & lack of focus; no clear implementation plan and over-reliance on vision statements. Strategy-40 provides a clear diagnosis of Meta but lacks some details on implementation as addressed in through the frame works. It aligns with Thiel and Masters' (2014, pp.10-17) Zero to One, which underscores the importance of creating breakthrough innovations rather than competing in existing markets. Meanwhile, Kim and Mauborgne's (2015, pp.3-8) Blue Ocean Strategy suggest that companies should create uncontested market space, rather than competing in saturated industries, a principle Meta applies by expanding into the metaverse and open-source AI. Overall it is a medium strength strategy.

pages.text: I. Introduction This assessment is focused on discussing negotiation as a vital life skill balancing communication, judgement, decision-making, and conflict resolution. As outlined in the Negotiations Lab course (De Rond, 2025), it involves both rational and intuitive problem-solving across various contexts. This work reflects on my diary, integrating insights from real-world case studies and simulations. It examines preparation, framing, and emotional intelligence in resolving conflicts, improving decision-making, and enabling cooperation across industries and international settings. It also includes learnings from plenary sessions featuring a distinguished astronaut and an MP discussing Brexit negotiations. By this assessment, I am pleased to confirm that I have thoroughly covered the five core books from the required reading: Fisher, Ury & Patton (2011), Kahneman (2011), Malhotra (2016), Stone, Patton & Heen (1999), and Voss (2016). These works provided complementary perspectives on negotiation, communication, and decisionmaking. Initially sceptical about the effectiveness of a negotiation "Lab" given time and resource constraints, I found that peer interactions and lecture reflections significantly enriched my learning. II. Strategies Evaluation Below are shown the different strategies highlighted during the course and linked to the respective negotiation sessions. Negotiate based on Interests A consistent approach recommended by Fisher, Ury and Patton (2011, pp.40-48) was to negotiate under interests and not positions. This process seemed to be applied successfully for the Salt Harbor Scenario (Wheeler, 2002). While negotiating a real estate development deal balancing financial interests and long-term community impact, a rational approach was likely to govern this situation given the clear interests of both parts. There was a set of incremental concessions as described by Martin, Goldstein, and Cialdini (2014, pp.115-117) to ensure that both entities were satisfied. The outcome was satisfactory, but sometime addressing interest is not enough this as presented in some of the upcoming scenarios. Reframing and empathic negotiation MedLee's scenario (Lun and Salacuse, 2018) on establishing a joint venture between American and Asian firms while managing was a good testing context for negotiating given cultural and strategic differences. Malhotra (2016, pp.121-124) refers to the effectiveness on presenting interests within the right framing and authentic empathy. Witnessing how both parts were getting frustrated on not moving on executive board and evaluating performance from the Lee family, further context was required to 85

ensure that there was a clear strategy derived from a respectful identity and learning conversation as recommended by Stone, Patton and Heen (1999, pp.14-17). The results were reached by the end of the negotiation ensuring that the Lees could maintain their identity while staying flexible and dynamic for the venture with MedDevice. Negotiate with interests, mediation and emotions. The PowerScreen contract dispute (Patton, Gordon & Clarkson, 2018) highlighted the role of emotions in negotiations alongside royalties, financial terms, and business continuity. The video played during the class demonstrated that emotions played a crucial role, yet the dispute had a clear cause. Fisher and Shapiro (2005, pp. 15-30) stress addressing concerns before emotions. Hacker sought recognition as well as financial compensation. As his lawyer, I highlighted his concerns, advocating for understanding before shifting focus to keeping the company running. Without mediation, dissolution was likely. I framed the situation as a misunderstanding, aligning with Star's interests (Ashford & Detert, 2015), ensuring cooperation (Lax & Sebenius, 1986, pp. 261-278), and fostering a successful agreement (Moore, 2014, pp. 477-486). We kept both the company and their relationship. Coalition forming in negotiations The Grand Afroport negotiation (Mehta, 2017) required applying new skills to secure a public-private partnership for airport infrastructure. The focus was on finding a solution that balanced most interests. Greene (1998, pp. 250-256) highlights coalitionbuilding as a strategy to strengthen influence, leverage power, and isolate opposition. This approach helped three parties reach consensus while marginalising a less cooperative player. Once the coalition formed, mutually beneficial solutions became easier to achieve, enabling teamwork even in high-stakes negotiations (Maxwell, 2007, pp. 255-259). Ultimately, the negotiation resulted in agreement on building the port, with one party being excluded as a consequence of seeking only their top desired interests. Security (and empathy) consensus on negotiations This strategy was used to handle the most emotionally and intellectually demanding negotiation (according to most peers). The WTC reconstruction negotiation (Susskind et al., 2019) caused friction as some students had personal ties to the real event. One player deviated from their role, framing arguments through a nationalistic lens. The student ignored instructions for their role and felt significantly involved and aimed to get the mediator to shared specific views against other players. Team members addressed the identity concerns mentioned above with emotional intelligence, following Fisher and Shapiro's (2005, pp. 129-146) approach. Kahneman

86

(2011, pp. 31-38) stresses the need to resist System 1 thinking and remain rational. Despite the emotional remarks from this student, the approach wad to listen, acknowledge and reframe their role to follow the instructions for their role. A respectful identity conversation took place with the student, as advised by Stone, Patton, and Heen (1999, pp. 111-117), ensured emotions were acknowledged. Finally, the team built coalitions and reached an option satisfying most parties. III. Self-learning Below are some key insights I gained about myself while reflecting on the negotiations. Importance of preparation: It was clear based on interactions on all the exercises about preparing well enough for the task to be done strengthens any talent as stated Maxwell, J.C. (2007, pp.83-88). Reading in detail about the cases, and then access to related news, allowed me to leverage key information during the negotiations. Unfortunately for their learning, underperformers during the negotiations tended to use GenAI to get summaries of the instructions and their positions. Do not make assumptions: The PowerScreen scenario had a very strong bias context by watching the video. From my perspective there was a strong assumption that Hacker was a very emotional reactive character. As his lawyer, I ensured that our negotiation was based on understanding the psychology behind Star as the manager as recommended by Lax (1986, pp.261-268), allowing us to eliminate assumptions about his Hacker's behaviour. Have a clear objective and quantifiable framework: As addressed by Kahneman (2011, pp.212-221) having a focused quantifiable framework (in my case using spreadsheets with weighted calculations) allowed me to use System 2 more efficiently and removed the noise. As introduced in the course having also a framework on 9 relevant dimensions in a worksheet (De Rond, 2025) to assess the negotiation parties played critical. Framing information is key: Kahneman and MP. In the first two negotiations, I tended to provide my positions and interests very straight forward. I realised that it is critical to present options to my counter parts in the right sequence and context as suggested by Malhotra (2016, pp.121-124). Likewise, by preparing the decision makers by giving them relevant information with enough anticipation, prevents them to felt rushed, with a sense of ownership as it was the case for influencing PM as Margaret Thatcher and Tony Blair (Wilson, 2025). Leverage your information and power: Although it was not possible to read other player instructions, it was critical from my side to let my counterparts to speak more than me applying the 70:30 rule suggested by professional negotiators in hostage situations (Brooks, 2025). I.e. during the Afroport case, I gained enough information to understand that my role as the Bank was the strongest with the enablement to veto the whole exercise if there was not a satisfactory outcome, and leverage that power with boldness, as ruled in by Greene (1998, pp 423-430). 87

IV. Learning from others Assertive Communication: During the WTC exercise, and the student getting emotional, it was critical to assert authentic empathy only we I had experienced a similar circumstance. We were careful on stating "I can only imagine how hard could this be to you and your closed ones" similar to security negotiations (Brookes, 2025). Be-aware of saboteurs: As highlighted by Greene in terms of people wearing masks (2018, pp.70-78), there can several reasons for saboteurs to be present in a group. This was a relevant out of the box realisation I had from the Afroport case. Unfortunately, it was too late to know it was the environmentalist during the exercise. Identity is critical to address: MedLee scenario, proved to have the Lee family role to be very reactive, and settle on their ways of doing business as a family. It took several iterations to ensure they understood the position from MedDevice under the right arguments and while understanding and keeping their identity as covered by Stone, Patton and Heen (1999, pp.116-117). Emotional Intelligence is fundamental: Fisher and Shapiro (2005, pp 147-152) let me reflect on using emotions constructively during the WTC exercise. Likewise, I was inspired by how a high-ranking public officer (Wilson, 2025) was not emotionally involved in critical decisions for national security during September 11 attacks. Within a calculated and prudent approach, he decided towards evacuating a critical building in London, and provide calm and cooperative direction at 10 Downing St. Build syndicates if relevant: Power sharing is relevant to form coalitions leading to consensus as highlighted by Greene (2018, pp.251-256). Both in the Afroport and WTC reconstruction this was critical. I managed to first listen to those who were more benefitted by my Bank and Developer roles, respectively, and form a small coalition to push for our share interests but also aimed to satisfy at least most of everyone's requirements. Fully differentiate preferable from not acceptable: As recommended by Fisher, Ury and Patton (2011, pp.40-48) it is critical to negotiate addressing the underlying interests rather than the represented roles. The WTC was almost failing as a negotiation since some team members focused more on their positions and actual nationalities rather than facts and interests. The whole negotiation changed when it we differentiate preferable outcomes from not-acceptable at all given our interests.

Plenary Sessions This diary assessment would not be completed without commenting on our plenary sessions.

88

Astronaut and ISS Training: Teamwork, negotiation, and communication are crucial for ISS astronauts to coordinate tasks, resolve conflicts, and ensure mission success (Metclaf-Lindenburger, 2025). Effective collaboration enhances safety, problemsolving, and international cooperation in the high-stakes space environment. Critical, on-time and factual communication is critical to ensuring saving lives in high performing elite teams as highlighted by Willink and Babin (2015, pp.83-89). Brexit Negotiations: A detailed narrative was presented on how David Cameron's Brexit was a failed strategy. It lacked clear risk assessment, over-relied on polls, misjudged public sentiment, and failed contingency planning post-referendum (Bilmoria, 2025) with Lord Bilmoria. Brexit negotiations needed clearer trade terms, realistic timeframes, and proactive solutions for Northern Ireland's border to prevent disruptions. Framing in public service is critical (Wilson, 2025) and Cameron should have taken a full ownership of this outcome as recommended by Willink and Babin (2015, pp.37-42) showing poor leadership execution. Instead, a chaotic succession of PMs lacked solid strategies to reach in time a good deal with the EU.

V. Conclusion

This assessment has provided valuable insights into negotiation strategies, including interest-based bargaining, reframing, mediation, coalition-building, and emotional intelligence. By applying theories from key readings such as Fisher, Ury & Patton (2011), Kahneman (2011), Malhotra (2016), and Greene (1998), I have developed a deeper understanding of effective negotiation techniques across various contexts. The case studies reinforced the importance of preparation, strategic framing, and adapting to cultural and emotional dynamics. Exercises such as the Salt Harbor and MedLee scenarios highlighted how addressing interests rather than positions leads to constructive outcomes. The PowerScreen dispute and WTC negotiations underscored the critical role of emotional intelligence, as outlined by Fisher & Shapiro (2005). Meanwhile, the Afroport case demonstrated coalition-building's effectiveness in highstakes settings (Maxwell, 2007). Reflections on self-learning highlighted the need for structured preparation, avoiding assumptions, and leveraging decision-making frameworks (Kahneman, 2011). Plenary sessions, particularly those on Brexit and astronaut training, reinforced leadership, risk assessment, and crisis communication lessons. Overall, this experience has enhanced my ability to navigate complex negotiations, combining rational problem-solving with strategic adaptability. By integrating theoretical knowledge with practical application, I have strengthened my negotiation skills for both professional and real-world scenarios. 89

1. Solution Outline Our team solution specifies Green Data's strategy for achieving sustainable data centre operations, focusing on AI, alternative energy, and efficient infrastructure. Our key points were: •

AI for Sustainability - We exposed that AI-driven optimisations aim to reduce emissions and energy consumption in data centres. AI-powered fleet management and predictive maintenance for driverless vehicles improve energy efficiency, while AI-driven workload distribution in data centres minimises power waste.

•

Alternative Energy Sources - The plan addressed transitioning data centres to renewable energy. Solar power is prioritised due to cost-effectiveness, with coinvestment in solar farms in southern England. Additional renewable options, including tidal and wind power, are considered for scalability.

•

Strategic Data Centre Planning - Our proposal included deploying underwater data centres to leverage natural cooling, reducing energy consumption. AIenhanced workload management will dynamically optimise computing resources, while smart cooling systems and heat reuse will cut water and power use.

Green Data partners with SAC and ARM to accelerate renewable energy adoption and energy-efficient AI hardware integration. The overarching goal is to achieve net-zero emissions by 2030 through our proposed sustainable initiatives, and a long-term commercial plan up to 2034.

2. Discussion Context Our project was based framework for our analysis for the Green Data challenge was introduced during our second lecture (Barret, 2025). We considered the capabilities of ARM across relevant industries including Driverless Cars and low power chips. Consequently, it was relevant for us to consider using their technologies for the datacentre of our hypothetical company. Renewable solar energies provided by SAC (Alves, 2025) was the second commercial consideration. Green Data had a major objective: reducing the environmental impact of their data centres specially those executing the AI algorithmic planning for driverless cars. Such ambitious objective for agile data driven organisation ready to innovate at high scale and fast pace is defined as a Massive-Transformative-Purpose (MTP) for Green Data (Ismail et al, 2014). The key reason to use AI in the driverless vehicles was focused to improved safety, reduced traffic congestion, and enhanced fuel efficiency (Tegmark, 2017). 93

Our business plan considered Green Data readiness for the upcoming innovations in transportation and prepare for global expansion while considering the technological trends and market forces (Osterwalder and Pigneur, 2010). For instance, the major economies besides UK, such as US and China are investing significantly into new technologies applied on roads, energy efficiency and AI implementation in driverless vehicles. Some of the benefits will be reducing energy consumption and road fatalities (Lee, 2018). Environmental Impact challenges According to relevant tech trends, Cloud Computing growth among top players is decreasing but investment on GenAI is increasing significantly together with overall R&D for those players (CB Insights, 2023). This helps to understand that Green Data investment on data servers would be focused mainly on the GenAI and AI powering the driverless cars rather than only using cloud services. Based on the focus on GenAI for our company, there are some key facts to consider about growth of energy demand for the AI data centres and hence environmental impact. On one hand it is claimed that some AI tasks do not consume too much energy. For instance, AI writing a page of text and generating images emit 130x and 310x less CO2 respectively than a human created material. DeepMind reduces Google's energy consumption in data centres by 30% (Tomlinson et al, 2023). On the other hand, there 8000 data centres in the World and energy consumption is expected to double from 2022 to 2026. Training an GenAI model generates the same CO2 than 5 standard cars during their whole lifespan (Marr, 2024). In terms of water, Google had a major controversy in Chile for a data centre pulling 170 litres/second in a populated area prone to draughts (DW News, 2024). Resourcefully, ARM has addressed those challenges through high energy-efficient processors. This was inspired based on data centre cases in Ireland, US (Ashton, 2023), while countries like Singapore restricting construction of those centres. Cooling and energy opportunities We decided to work with SAC, based on their successful implementation on building a 5MW solar farm (Alves, 2025). A challenge would be UK's reduced sunlight availability, so we adjusted our calculations for our facility in Southern UK with relative lower solar exposure but bigger facility to reduce 70k-tonnes CO2 emissions for 20242034. The case of the Horsey Levels solar farm is a successful case of a large solar farm in the South of England just 4 miles away from the sea (National Grid. (2024). Another opportunity identified was the placing of our data centre underwater and in the proximity solar farm situated by the coast. A successful case by Microsoft took place in Scotland, a data centre 117 feet deep to the seafloor (Microsoft, 2020). This would mean for our data centre: efficient cooling and less losses on energy transmission while close to the farm.

94

Data Centres and AI The usage of natural water streams and AI algorithms to reduce environmental impact is another opportunity. For instance, Meta aiming to reduce their net emissions of 7.4M tonnes of CO2, uses river resources with fish passages to cool down their data centres (Climate Insider, 2024). In terms of AI, Meta is using Reinforcement Learning methods to optimise the allocation of energy and cooling resources (InfoQ, 2024). This goes in accordance with how AI systems can predict and adjust to changing demands, leading to reduced energy consumption and costs (Tegmark, 2017). New electronic design is another opportunity we can leverage. AI can work locally in a device reducing energy consumption (Clark, 2024). ARM new chip designs applied on low energy consumption (Fotheringham and Teich, 2021) can be used on both the vehicles and the data centres. Conclusion Given the opportunities and challenges presented above, we proposed a plan for Green Data to minimise data centre environmental impact, especially for AI in driverless cars. Using ARM's low-power chips and SAC's solar energy, we explored sustainable cooling, AI-driven optimisation, and innovative electronic designs to reduce CO2 emissions and energy consumption efficiently. Preliminary Deal Analysis Market Sentiment Analysis Case Study

Market Sentiment Analysis AI is used to analyses news, social media and other media to detect trends and tone changes across assets and regions.

Redfin recognised the need to enhance its market analysis capabilities beyond traditional data sources.

Tools have been developed to track big data sets such as consumer reviews to identify changing tenant preferences and neighbourhood sentiment.

They developed an AI-enabled market sentiment analysis tool to analyse customer reviews.

This use-case of AI delivers early signals of market momentum to support smarter investment decisions ahead of lagging indicators like leasing or transaction data.

AI sentiment analysis enabled Redfin to interpret emotional tone and market trends from diverse textual sources, offering early indicators of market shifts before traditional data reflects them.

Efficiency In Due Diligence Lease Abstraction Case Study

Lease Abstraction A review of lease documentation is an essential part of any due diligence process.

Seattle-based URG (14M sf portfolio) used Prophia in their recent acquisition of a retail mall.

Machine learning models have been trained on thousands of lease agreements and provide accurate data, cost savings and efficient lease abstractions.

The AI-powered lease abstraction software was used to review 100 tenant leases in a 10-day DD period.

Traditionally this was done by lawyers, and often took days, but now can be done in hours.

The process quickly identified 20+ documents that were missing and critical questions that URG needed resolved by the seller.

The lease abstracts provided by Prophia were beneficial in expediting the review of Argus files, enhancing the valuation and cash flow forecasting process.

Case Studies Enhancing Sustainable Real Estate Investing Through AI in Valuations Norway's SWF

CoreLogic, Australia Automated Valuation Models AI driven AVMs were used to process vast datasets swiftly, resulting in more accurate property valuations. Their AVM Explorer tool allows users to delve into factors influencing a property's estimated value, enhancing confidence in valuations. This reduces the need for redundant site visits and physical inspections while optimising land usage.

Thinking Outside the Black Box

Reconstruct a Structured AI Judgement Process

Redefining Explainability in AI-Driven Investment Decisions The unsolvable AI black box problem: April 3rd, Anthropic published their latest research further confirming that existing AI explainability is a pseudo-concept in their groundbreaking paper "Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think" .

Redefining explainability

Rethinking Explainability

Why does it matter

1. When we talk about explainability, what are we really talking about? True Intentions: Technical breakthrough? To create greater value in real-world business contexts? 2. A thinking dilemma rather than a dead end： A formalism trap caused by "technological solutionism"

Because the Black Box issue Kills Trust For BR: For the same question: 1.AI gives you an answer---->How can I explain to investors why this answer is credible? 2. AI gives you another answer: How do I explain this inconsistency to investors?

1. A Redefinition: Explainability = Priceability 2. A Practical Approach： Design a verification and reasoning framework capable of assessing the reliability of outputs produced by large language models (LLMs)

3. The truly unavoidable question： What kind of rationale-backed AI decision-making process would produce answers that clients would actually buy into?

For BR's clients: 1.Why should I choose/trust BR instead of your competitors? 2. Does your investment decision suggestions make sense to me? (If so, how)

E.g., the BR model ——— A proprietary LLM co-developed with OpenAI. 3. The system should incorporate the following features: Explicit logic chain (VS) The black-box nature Quantifiable risk assessment (VS) The randomness and volatility

For AI expert: No trust without understanding. No scale without trust.

Built-in adaptability for future scenarios

2. Validation phase: Stress testing + causal inference

Risk Assessment

Assessing Risks and Mitigation Actions on GenAI

Risk for Real Estate Investor and Decision Maker

Reputational Risk for Real Estate Investment Company

Financial Risk for Real Estate Investment Company

Risk for Workforce of Real Estate Investment Company

Legal/Regulation Risk for Real Estate Investment Company

Minor

Risk: Overreliance on black-box AI outputs may mislead individual investors. Mitigation: Use AI tools with interpretable outputs and human-in-the-loop oversight.

Risk: Public scepticism if model outputs lack transparency. Mitigation: Publish model explainability reports.

Risk: Slight inefficiencies from suboptimal but explainable models. Mitigation: Balance performance with interpretability.

Risk: Confusion or lack of trust in AI tools. Mitigation: Provide training on explainable AI principles.

Risk: Non-compliance with soft guidelines. Mitigation: Monitor evolving explainability standards.

Moderate

Risk: Inaccurate intermediate outputs may lead to poor investment choices. Mitigation: Validate models using scenario testing and feature attribution tools.

Risk: Criticism from media or clients over opaque decision-making. Mitigation: Engage in stakeholder co-design and communications training.

Risk: Investment losses from feature attribution errors. Mitigation: Use reliable techniques (e.g., decision trees) and expert validation.

Risk: Job displacement due to misunderstood AI roles. Mitigation: Involve staff in AI adoption and re-skill accordingly.

Risk: Breaches of transparency obligations. Mitigation: Use interpretable models and log decision rationale.

High

Risk: Misinterpretation of generative AI insights could drive systemic misallocation of capital. Mitigation: Apply explainability techniques like counterfactuals and external auditing.

Risk: Public backlash from biased or unexplained model predictions. Mitigation: Incorporate diverse datasets and regular ethical reviews.

Risk: Major losses from reliance on hallucinated LLM outputs. Mitigation: Use multiagent and retrievalaugmented systems to reduce error.

Risk: Workforce resistance or disengagement. Mitigation: Apply participatory design methods to integrate human expertise.

Risk: Legal penalties due to non-compliance with AI laws. Mitigation: Align AI development with regulatory frameworks and conduct legal audits.

Impact

Safeguarding Generative AI A hybrid approach using rule-based and classifier ML guardrails for safe, accurate Responses Real estate conversations must respect fair housing laws that prohibit discriminatory practices, such as "steering" potential buyers or renters toward or away from properties based on protected characteristics (race, religion, disability, etc.). Pre-processor: Scans incoming user requests for potential non-compliance.

Post-processor: Validates the LLM's generated response before passing it on to the user.

3 Core Approach - current best practice is to blend all three. Prompt Engineering: • • •

Insert instructions in the system prompt that explicitly forbid discriminatory responses and remind the model to follow fair housing laws, using the RHODES Framework Advantage: Easy to implement, keeps many responses in compliance. Drawback: Can be overly cautious, mistakenly blocking legitimate requests (low precision).

Stop List: • • •

Maintain a list of high-severity, banned terms or phrases—if the model output or user input contains them, automatically refuse or filter the request. Advantage: Guarantees certain content never makes it through. Drawback: Lacks context—simple keyword matching can lead to errors (false positives).

Classifier Model: • • •

Build a specialised machine learning classifier (e.g., fine-tuned BERT) to detect potential fair housing violations in either the user's query or the LLM's response. Advantage: More nuanced and context-aware, tuneable precision/recall, and less likely to over-block. Drawback: Requires building and maintaining a labelled dataset, more complex engineering.

Prompt and Key Word Engineering Best Practices For best results with LLMs, be clear and specific, provide context and structure prompts logically. Ask for step-by-step reasoning, refine iteratively, and use examples to guide output. These practices help ensure more accurate, relevant and useful responses.

Provide Context

Ask for Step-by-Step Reasoning

Give background, role, or audience details to help the model tailor responses more accurately to your needs.

Encourage logical thinking by asking for stepby-step explanations, which improves accuracy and transparency in complex tasks.

Be Specific and Clear

Use Iterative Refinement

Use precise language and direct instructions to reduce ambiguity and guide the model towards the desired outcome.

Review, adjust, and clarify prompts based on output to progressively improve the quality and relevance of responses.

Use Structured Prompts

Leverage Few-Shot or Zero-Shot Examples

Organise requests using lists or sections to guide the model in producing well-formatted, easy-to-follow responses.

Show examples of ideal output to help the model learn and mimic the structure, tone, or format expected.

Successful Implementation of GenAI in Global Firm

Morgan Stanley Private ChatGPT

In 2023, Morgan Stanley implemented a private GPT-4 system for wealth management, enabling advisors to access internal insights and generate client-ready summaries securely, while maintaining compliance; setting a benchmark for secure, explainable GenAI use in financial investments.

03

Continuous Monitoring and Improvement

Domain-Specific Data for Training

Feedback loops for users to rate outputs and report inconsistencies were stablished; ensuring model evolved with market conditions and internal strategy.

The models were trained using high-quality, inhouse data related to property markets, asset performance, and financial metrics. Incorporated region-specific legal and tax considerations.

Embedded Explainability Features

Defined Clear Use Cases and Limitations

Explainability was integrated clarifying how the model arrives at suggestions. Summarisation prompts, source referencing, and visual aids were used to foster trust from stakeholders.

The models' scope was limited to assistive tasks such as market commentary. It was avoided letting it make final investment calls without human review, and transparent guardrails.

Involved Investment Tuning Experts

Data Privacy and Compliance

Human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning (RLHF) involved experienced investment professionals to fine-tune outputs and decision logic with institutional expectations.

ChatGPT was setup a secure, private environment; either on-premises or via a trusted cloud partner; with full compliance with data protection regulations (e.g. GDPR, CCPA).

Horizon 1 (Immediate, 0–1 Year)

AI-Augmented Underwriting and Due Diligence

Enhance Data Infrastructure

BlackRock should consolidate and clean its real estate data into a unified platform, creating a "CoStar-like" database of internal and external information.

Integrate AI in Deal Analysis

Use AI algorithms in underwriting models to rapidly analyse deals and market data, for instance by verifying property valuations alongside traditional appraisals.

Automate Due Diligence Tasks

Implement AI including reading AI for time-consuming due diligence tasks like reviewing leases, contracts and financial statements. By using proven software (as in the Prophia case), BlackRock can reduce time consuming in extracting key lease terms, flagging risks and identifying missing documents.

Improve Valuation and Underwriting Accuracy

Use AI for scenario analysis and risk flagging in underwriting. Models can run thousands of simulations (varying assumptions like lease-up periods, interest rates, or cap rates) to identify downside risks and flag anomalies by comparing against past deals.

Deploy AI Productivity Tools

Immediately equip investment teams with AI-driven productivity tools, such as natural language query interfaces (e.g., a chatGPT plugin) to quickly retrieve insights from BlackRock's databases. Also deploy interpretability tools like SHAP and LIME to ensure transparent predictions.

Extend application

Strengthen the foundation

Foster Ecosystem

Horizon 2 (Medium Term, 2–5 Years) Scalable AI-Driven Management Scale Data and Tech Infrastructure

As AI expands, BlackRock must scale infrastructure in Horizon 2 through cloud computing and robust governance. Partnerships with cloud providers or data firms can feed continuous property, market, and ESG data into models. Ensuring data privacy, model validation and ethical AI by training on segmented data and using synthetic inputs keeps decisions compliant and fair.

Build a Scalable AI Platform

BlackRock should establish an enterprise-level AI platform for real estate, following the lead of industry pioneers. This strategy could include creating a proprietary Real Estate LLM (Large Language Model) in partnership with OpenAI and using co-design methodologies to involve both staff and clients in model validation and interpretation. Such an approach would build stakeholder trust and foster a robust AI ecosystem.

Talent and Culture Development

By the medium term, BlackRock should have a dedicated AI-focused real estate team and training programs to upskill traditional professionals on AI outputs. Fostering a collaborative culture where AI is seen as a partner, rather than a threat, will help maximise its benefits.

Adopt the Structural Intelligence Framework

BlackRock can pilot the structural intelligence approach in underwriting and portfolio strategy, ensuring every investment decision is backed by an explainable AI "decision chain" that highlights both macro factors (GDP growth, AI adoption rate, interest rates) and micro factors (occupancy, energy efficiency, etc.).

AI-Driven Portfolio Management

With foundational tools in place, Horizon 2 shifts to portfolio-level optimisation. BlackRock can use AI to rebalance portfolios, optimise allocations and detect concentration risks or opportunities (e.g., tenant-type correlations with tech stocks). Real-time data feeds enable dynamic adjustments.

Horizon 3 (Long Term, 5+ Years) AI-Driven Strategic Transformation and New Opportunities

Investing in AI-Centric Assets and Infrastructure

Embed AI Fully in Strategic and Investment Decision-Making

By this stage, AI will reshape real estate demand, prompting BlackRock to tilt its portfolio toward digital infrastructure (data centres, cloud facilities, telecom sites). AI will also boost demand for life sciences labs and tech incubator spaces, so BlackRock should ensure adequate exposure to these sectors. BlackRock can create advanced AI forecasting models with synthetic data to imagine future states. Instead of standard 10-year proformas, a Horizon-3 approach might use a perpetual digital twin, fed by real data and AI-generated scenarios (economic, demographic, climate), to continuously simulate outcomes. Beyond forecasting, agentic GenAI can support multi-source due diligence and personalise investor updates. AI might also enable fundamentally new ways to invest in and own real estate, and BlackRock should be prepared to innovate here. We might see the rise of tokenised real estate platforms where AI facilitates fractional ownership and liquidity, or AI-driven marketplaces matching global investors to assets in real-time.

New Investment and Ownership Models

Aligning with Emerging Urban Infrastructure Needs

By aligning investments with the infrastructure of the future (digital, transportation, and energy), BlackRock ensures its portfolio remains relevant and valuable as cities modernise in the AI era.
