BlackRock GCP: AI in Real Estate

1

Executive Summary The Global Consulting Project was conducted for BlackRock's Global Real Estate Research team. It is aimed to explore the transformative role of Artificial Intelligence in shaping the future of real estate investments. As the world's largest asset manager, BlackRock is uniquely positioned to lead on emerging technologies but with the rise of generative AI and machine learning comes both opportunity and uncertainty. The central question guiding our project was: "How can BlackRock responsibly and effectively adopt AI to enhance its real estate investment capabilities and decision-making processes?" The scope of the project covered three primary areas: (1) How AI is influencing real estate demand and human behaviour, (2) The application of AI within real estate investment strategy and (3) The risks and limitations associated with AI adoption. To answer these, we combined qualitative primary research, conducting interviews with AI experts, academics and real estate professionals, with extensive secondary research that included academic publications, industry reports and real-world case studies. We also integrated feedback from our client and academic supervisor throughout the process. Our findings reveal that AI is acting as a fourth major wave of disruption in real estate, following mechanisation, urbanisation and globalisation. It is altering demand patterns across asset classes, enabling a shift from traditional valuation drivers to realtime, intelligence-driven metrics. Data centres, logistics hubs and life sciences facilities emerge as clear beneficiaries of AI's infrastructure needs, while traditional retail and office spaces face headwinds unless repositioned with tech-enhanced services. We identified a wide range of AI applications already delivering value across the real estate investment lifecycle. These include AI-powered tools for lease abstraction, deal underwriting, sentiment-based market analysis and advanced risk forecasting using machine learning and geospatial data. AI also supports operational efficiency through GPT-powered document analysis and internal tools like JLL GPT. A key innovation we proposed is the Structured AI Judgment Process, a framework combining AI outputs with

119

BlackRock GCP: AI in Real Estate

2

quantitative validation and feedback loops to ensure transparency, explainability and strategic accountability. However, AI adoption also introduces challenges. These include data bias, regulatory compliance, lack of explainability and risks of overreliance on opaque models. To address these, we proposed a multi-layered mitigation strategy, including prompt engineering best practices, stop lists, classifier models and human-in-the-loop oversight. We highlighted Morgan Stanley's Private ChatGPT system as a benchmark example of responsible, institution-aligned AI deployment. To guide BlackRock's strategic approach, we applied the Three-Horizon Framework, outlining a roadmap across short, medium and long-term opportunities. In Horizon 1 (0–1 year), we recommend enhancing data infrastructure and piloting proven AI tools. In Horizon 2 (2–5 years), we advise investing in scalable AI platforms, strategic partnerships and transparency frameworks. Horizon 3 (5+ years) focuses on embedding AI in strategic decision-making, portfolio rebalancing and investing in AI-era infrastructure such as digital twins. This report concludes that while AI presents significant complexity, it also offers BlackRock a powerful opportunity to lead the industry in responsible, data-driven innovation. With the right safeguards and governance, AI can be a critical enabler of competitive advantage in real estate investing. I. Aims This project aimed to explore the transformative role of AI in shaping the future of real estate investment and strategy for BlackRock. The focus lied in three core areas: 1. Understanding AI's Influence on Real Estate Demand and Human Behaviour To examine how AI-driven changes in consumer behaviour, lifestyle and business operations impact property valuations, location preferences and demand across various real estate classes.

120

BlackRock GCP: AI in Real Estate

3

2. Integrating AI into Investment Strategy To identify how AI technologies can be effectively applied to enhance the overall real estate investment. 3. Evaluating Risks and Challenges of AI Adoption To assess the key risks, regulatory and ethical concerns associated with AI integration in investment models and to develop practical mitigation strategies through a structured risk register, ensuring responsible and sustainable adoption. By conducting research across these three areas, we ultimately aimed to provide the client with strategic recommendations on the future disruptive impact of AI on real estate demand, effective ways to leverage AI and limitations of the risks associated with AI adoption. II. Context This project was commissioned by BlackRock Inc., the world's largest asset manager with nearly $12 trillion in assets under management as of December 2024. Against a backdrop of rapid technological advancement, increasing public interest in AI and growing regulatory scrutiny, BlackRock sought to explore how AI could be a source of competitive advantage for their global portfolio of direct investments in commercial real estate. The team at BlackRock who engaged us was the Real Estate Research Team, who actively assist investment teams across multiple geographies and asset classes. This team is especially focused on understanding long-term trends, particularly any trend which may impact real estate demand or portfolio stability. AI emerged as a priority topic for them not only because of its transformative potential but also due to its opacity and the emerging need for clear frameworks to evaluate its risks and opportunities. From a broader industry perspective, AI is already beginning to alter the structure of real estate markets, including how tenants interact with the built environment and how

121

BlackRock GCP: AI in Real Estate

4

investors identify and underwrite deals. For institutional investors such as BlackRock, this presents a need to capture the upside of AI-enhanced tools while navigating risks such as black-box algorithms, data privacy concerns and regulatory uncertainty. III. Methodology To answer key research questions set out for us, we used a combination of research approaches. This included qualitative primary research through expert interviews and quantitative & qualitative secondary research from academic and industry sources. This dual approach ensured both depth and breadth of research to cover the entire scope of all the key research questions. The team started by focusing on primary research, as we know that securing these interviews would be time-consuming and critical to providing unique insights for the client. We focused on three types of experts: academic researchers, industry professionals and AI-specific experts. This approach was adopted to ensure we gained a holistic understanding of how AI is currently utilised across the real estate industry and to explore the future implications for each asset class. The team utilised the Cambridge academic network, our own personal networks as well as the client network to achieve this. This process resulted in over thirty reach-outs, more than ten informal conversations and five formal research interviews. Two of the formal interviews were conducted with academic researchers, two with industry experts and one with an AI-specific expert, which accomplished our goal for a well-rounded group of interviews. All interviews were conducted using a questionnaire agreed upon by the team, with detailed notes taken and team debriefs afterwards to ensure that all information gathered was disseminated and analysed by all members of the team. Given BlackRock's extensive research capabilities and discussions had with them early in the process, we understood that secondary research would be less likely than primary research to provide the unique insights that they were looking for as part of the deliverables. As such, secondary research was undertaken primarily to broaden our understanding of trends, validate and support information found in primary research and

122

BlackRock GCP: AI in Real Estate

5

find case studies on AI adoption which may be of interest to our client. To conduct efficient secondary research, topics were broken down based on the key research questions and assigned to individual team members, with collaborative reviews happening every other day to share findings amongst the team. As information came to light via this process, the team applied the most insightful findings to each focus area of the PID. Critically, during the collaborative research reviews, the team also introduced original intellectual contributions and our own viewpoints on findings to exceed the client's expectations. Further improving the quality and depth of thinking were weekly meetings with the client, where we followed a structured agenda to review key findings and discuss topics of interest and weekly meetings with our academic supervisor where we talked through our research methods and uncovered new sources. IV. Analysis The process to move from research to concrete findings, results and recommendations included a mixed-methods approach, combining qualitative expert interviews with secondary data analysis and industry case studies. The first PID objective, how AI would influence real estate demand and human behaviour, was addressed by examining the results of perspectives from the primary research interviews, learning from past trends and corroborating them with macro-level trends obtained from secondary sources. The team focused on the likely impacts of these findings on to each major real estate asset class to create a matrix categorising asset class as "front runners", "marginal gainers" or "stragglers". Analysing the second objective, the potential for AI integration in BlackRock's investment strategy, required a more granular understanding of where AI could be used across a real estate investment workflow. The team focused on areas where AI integration could yield improvements in decision making accuracy or efficiency. Various use-cases were reviewed and their relevancy to BlackRock's process and strategy was contemplated.

123

BlackRock GCP: AI in Real Estate

6

The final objective, identifying risks and challenges with AI adoption, required the development of a risk matrix to cover operational, financial, reputational, workforce and legal risks. As risks were identified through research they were logged in the matrix and categorised and low, medium or high risk. Accompanying mitigations were included if preexisting or hypothesised by the team if not. From the risk analysis the concept of a structured AI judgement process was born. We found that one of the largest risks of AI adoption was that results came from a "black box" and were generally unexplainable. This posed a large issue for a company such as BlackRock who must disclose and explain decisions to investors, clients and the public. Therefore, we developed a model with a three-stage framework: data augmentation, hybrid AI-quantitative model integration and feedback loops. The underlying rationale was that AI outputs must be not only accurate but also explainable and "priceable", a distinction reflecting the importance of investor confidence in "black box" decision making. The analytical process consistently aligned with the PID's stated objectives, bridging the gap from exploration to making recommendations. By blending qualitative insight with real-world use-cases, the team delivered a set of strategic tools that were both innovative and applicable to our client. V. Results Understanding AI's Influence on Real Estate Demand and Human Behaviour Our research led us to conclude that AI represents the fourth major wave of disruption in real estate, following mechanisation, urbanisation, and globalisation. Unlike previous transformations, AI doesn't just change where and how people live and work but fundamentally reshapes the value drivers of real estate itself. As AI becomes increasingly intelligent and cost-effective, driven by exponential advancements and significant stepchanges in computing power (Slumbers, 2025), real-time intelligence, automation, and predictive analytics will continue to transform how assets are valued, operated, and exited.

124

BlackRock GCP: AI in Real Estate

7

This shift is producing winners and losers among asset classes (Anderson, 2025). Data centres are clear front-runners, propelled by surging demand for digital infrastructure to support AI models. Logistics assets also benefit from AI-optimised supply chains and the expansion of e-commerce. Similarly, life sciences and healthcare spaces are in demand due to their alignment with innovation economies and university clusters. In contrast, traditional office and retail assets face growing structural risk. AIenabled remote work and virtual collaboration are reducing the need for physical office space. Similarly, AI-driven e-commerce is accelerating the decline of brick-and-mortar retail. Without strategic repositioning, these assets risk obsolescence (Slumbers, 2025). For BlackRock, the implication is clear: portfolio exposure must be adjusted toward techaligned, service-oriented and future-resilient assets. More broadly, Lindenthal (2025) believed that real estate is becoming increasingly service centric. AI enables buildings to function as dynamic, responsive environments rather than static structures. Landlords are expected to behave more like service providers, delivering personalisation, operational efficiency and real-time feedback. For investors, asset management capabilities are now just as important as acquisition decisions. AI Applications: Enhancing the Investment Lifecycle AI is delivering real, measurable benefits across the real estate investment lifecycle, from deal sourcing, underwriting to asset management and exit planning. Its core value lies in improving data-driven decision-making, operational efficiency and the ability to uncover early market signals. In underwriting and due diligence, massive efficiency gains are made through a multitude of tools. One example highlighted was AI-powered lease abstraction though a case study where a US-based real estate firm used AI to review hundreds of tenant leases in only a few days during due-diligence, identifying over missing documents and supporting more accurate cash flow projections (Prophia, 2024). Another example shown was GPT-

125

BlackRock GCP: AI in Real Estate

8

powered tools to enhance productivity by turning plain text into Excel formulas and summarising complex documents, making early-stage deal underwriting faster and more accessible (GPTExcel, n.d.). Market analysis is also evolving with AI-enabled sentiment tools. Redfin, for instance, developed a system that scans reviews, news and social media to detect neighbourhood trends before they appear in transaction data, giving investors an informational edge (Hintz, 2022). One of the most powerful applications of AI is its transformative impact on risk analysis. Advanced machine learning and natural language processing are being used to identify, quantify and simulate diverse risk types, ranging from market volatility and property depreciation to environmental and legal risks. For example, predictive models can run thousands of simulations to estimate downside exposure. Geospatial AI highlights climate risks like flooding or wildfire exposure, while computer vision tools such as ZestyAI's "Roof Age" assess physical asset risk via satellite images (ZestyAI, n.d.). Across all these cases, high-quality, integrated data is foundational. Platforms like CoStar and CoreLogic centralise vast property datasets, supporting better forecasting and valuation. CoreLogic's AI-powered automatic valuation models, for example, enhance valuation confidence by allowing users to explore the drivers behind each estimate (CoreLogic, 2022). Firms are also embedding AI directly into internal operations. JLL GPT, a proprietary language model, empowers brokers with instant insights and speeds up document analysis, boosting both efficiency and client service (JLL, 2024). Together, these applications show how AI, when paired with high-quality data and explainability, can enhance both investment speed and confidence. Evaluating Risks and Challenges of AI Adoption While AI offers substantial benefits to real estate investment, it also introduces critical risks and limitations, particularly around transparency, bias and responsible use. For institutional investors like BlackRock, ensuring that AI tools are trustworthy, explainable and compliant with regulations is essential.

126

BlackRock GCP: AI in Real Estate

9

A central challenge is explainability. Many AI systems, especially large language models, operate as black boxes, making it difficult to justify investment recommendations. This undermines both internal confidence and client trust. Tools like Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) help address this issue. SHAP visualises which features most influenced a model's decision, while LIME offers plain-language explanations for specific outputs, such as why one property was preferred over another (Keita, 2023). A more advanced application is the structured AI judgment process, which integrates AI outputs with quantitative validation to ensure assumptions (like IRR or utility costs) are transparent and testable. Another key limitation is biases in training data. Real estate models often rely on datasets that may be incomplete or historically skewed, such as overrepresentation of major cities or legacy pricing patterns (Boeing, 2019). To mitigate this, firms must audit data sources, diversify training inputs and use synthetic data to test for edge cases and underrepresented segments. Data need to be consistent and thorough (Lindenthal, 2025). Compliance and ethics are also major concerns, particularly in real estate, where regulations like fair housing laws prohibit discriminatory practices. By designing prompts that explicitly prohibit bias, using stop lists to block high-risk terms and deploying classifier models to screen AI outputs, firms can prevent unintended violations while preserving model flexibility (National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2022). Strong data governance and diversity are foundational, along with prioritising model explainability through transparent algorithms and summarisation prompts. These steps help ensure AI systems remain both compliant and trusted. A standout example is Morgan Stanley's custom ChatGPT, which used internal training data, built-in explainability and human reinforcement learning to align AI recommendations with institutional standards, proving responsible AI adoption is achievable at scale (Morgan Stanley, 2023).

127

BlackRock GCP: AI in Real Estate

10

Ultimately, these practices are not just safeguards, they position BlackRock to adopt AI confidently, ethically and competitively in a rapidly evolving investment landscape. VI. Recommendations We analysed BlackRock's key competitive advantages and in response to the inherent uncertainty surrounding AI implication and adoption applied the Three-Horizon Framework (Baghai, Coley and White, 1999, p. 45) to strategically manage their allocation of resources and attention across current, emerging and future opportunities. In Horizon 1 (Immediate Term, 0-1 year), the recommendation emphasised investing in the foundational aspects of AI, primarily enhancing data infrastructure by consolidating and cleaning real estate data into a unified platform, akin to a "CoStar-like" database. Additionally, it suggests launching pilot projects in AI applications that have demonstrated maturity in the market. This includes integrating AI algorithms into deal analysis for rapid market data and property valuation verification, automating due diligence tasks through proven AI software such as reading AI for leases, contracts and financial statements and employing AI-driven scenario analysis for risk detection and anomaly identification. These pilot initiatives are complemented by productivity tools equipped with natural language query interfaces and interpretability tools like SHAP and LIME to ensure transparent AI-driven predictions (Ribeiro et al., 2016). Horizon 2 (Medium Term, 2-5 years) centres on enhancing the foundational AI infrastructure, fostering a collaborative ecosystem through partnerships and closely collaborating with clients to co-develop AI applications. This involves further scaling the infrastructure by leveraging cloud computing, implementing robust data engineering and governance practices, and forming strategic partnerships with leading cloud and AI providers such as OpenAI. These collaborations can enable seamless integration, ensure model validation, and mitigate the risks associated with developing in-house models that may quickly become obsolete (Szumilo, 2025). Developing talent through targeted training programs will ensure the workforce is adequately equipped to leverage AI effectively.

128

BlackRock GCP: AI in Real Estate

11

Additionally, enhancing AI transparency by adopting the structural intelligence framework will be critical. Subsequently, AI applications will be extended into more advanced use cases such as scalable AI-driven portfolio management, real-time allocation optimisation and dynamic portfolio rebalancing based on real-time data feeds. In Horizon 3 (Long Term, 5+ years), we anticipated AI-driven strategic transformation and new opportunities. Investments will shift even more towards AI-centric digital infrastructure such as data centres, cloud facilities and telecom sites. BlackRock should position itself strategically to meet rising demands in life sciences labs and technology incubator spaces. The long-term vision includes embedding AI deeply into strategic and investment decision-making processes, utilising advanced AI forecasting with synthetic data, perpetual digital twins and personalised investor updates through agentic generative AI (Romero-Cano, 2025). Lastly, aligning BlackRock's investments with emerging urban infrastructure needs covering digital, transportation and energy sectors, will ensure portfolio relevance and sustainable growth in the AI era. Through this strategic roadmap, BlackRock will progressively build robust capabilities, capitalise on immediate opportunities and strategically position itself for long-term growth driven by advanced AI integration. VII. Challenges A key challenge of this project was the broad scope. We were tasked with examining the impact of artificial intelligence on society and linking these changes to trends in real estate investment. At the same time, we assessed how artificial intelligence is currently applied in investment strategy, identified associated risks and proposed ways to address them. The work involved both large-scale analysis, such as shifts in human behaviour and the influence of artificial intelligence on economic structures, and detailed strategic advice for a global asset manager. The PID also included complex questions on asset management, such as how artificial intelligence might enhance interactions with the built environment to improve operational efficiency. However, as the project progressed, the client advised us to concentrate on the investment-focused applications of artificial

129

BlackRock GCP: AI in Real Estate

12

intelligence. As a result, operational aspects were addressed only briefly in the appendix of the presentation sent to the client and excluded from the results mentioned above. Another major challenge was conducting interviews with a wide variety of stakeholders. Given the overlap of artificial intelligence and real estate investment, it was essential to engage with individuals from a range of fields, including institutional investors, artificial intelligence experts, and academic researchers. Scheduling these discussions proved difficult, with time zone differences, limited availability and the need to tailor each conversation to the interviewee's expertise. It took significant effort to identify suitable contacts, craft personalised outreach messages and align interviews with our developing research structure. Consequently, these constraints resulted in a relatively low number of interviews, limiting the breadth of insights we could directly gather. The cross-disciplinary nature of the topic also required us to interpret unfamiliar technical terminology and communicate it in a way that was relevant to business. Concepts such as model explainability, synthetic data and prompt engineering needed to be understood in enough depth to explain clearly to real estate professionals. At the same time, our recommendations had to be practical and aligned with the operational context of a company like BlackRock. Balancing technical insight with strategic relevance was challenging but ultimately rewarding. To address these issues, our team adopted a proactive and cooperative approach. From the beginning, we maintained close communication with the client, which helped guide and shape our research. In terms of interviews, we made use of all available networks, including personal contacts, our academic supervisors and introductions from the client. This enabled us to reach qualified individuals through artificial intelligence, investment and academia. We created a standard interview guide to ensure consistency across conversations. Throughout the process, we also integrated feedback from our supervisor, particularly when refining technical content into useful business advice. This ongoing feedback loop allowed us to improve our narrative and deliver insights that were both robust and practical.

CEO Leadership Reflection – NVIDIA in the times of aggressive growth and challenges

In May 2023, following the departure of Jensen Huang, a transformative leader in the history of NVIDIA, a new era began for this hugely innovative organisation and for my career. Assuming the role of CEO after a founder of a stature like Steve Jobs or Bill Gates required not only a continuation of strategic excellence but also a redefinition of leadership for the next phase of the company's exponential trajectory. Over this period, I have applied successfully the "Unique Work of the CEO" framework from Feigen Advisors (2023) and enabled key strategies on three foundational elements from the "7 Powers" according to Helmer (2016) which are Switching Costs, Branding and Process Power. Consequently, this has enabled sustaining and growing NVIDIA's global impact through these last 24 months despite major challenges as summarised below. Setting the Vision, the Strategy, and the Plan; Driving Execution Upon taking leadership at NVIDIA, I re-evaluated our vision by applying Porter's (1979) five competitive forces: industry rivalry, threats from new entrants and substitutes, and supplier and buyer power. With rising competition from firms like DeepSeek, I defined a forward-looking vision to deepen NVIDIA's defensible resources. These include our Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA) ecosystem, data centre leadership, and expansion into areas such as Generative AI infrastructure. Strategically, I prioritised differentiation and cost leadership through tighter hardware-software integration and proprietary AI models to reduce third-party dependence. Partnerships with governments and cloud providers have helped neutralise substitute threats, while vertical integration, including the acquisition of key intellectual property, has reduced dependency on suppliers. This clarity has guided our resource allocation and market focus. Talent retention has been central to our strategy, inspired by Reed Hastings' principles of talent density, fair pay, and context over control (Hastings, 2020). In the past year, 231 high-calibre Intel employees joined NVIDIA, accounting for 9.24 percent of new hires, as we maintained top-tier compensation (Munyikwa, 2024) as shown in figure 1.

Figure 1. Average salaries of current GPU-related U.S. employees in September 2024 (Munyikwa, 2024)

Execution centres on decentralised innovation teams with defined KPIs, strong talent acquisition, and fast iteration cycles. Porter's framework has informed every decision layer, supporting a resilient and adaptive leadership approach that empowers our executive team. Setting the Capital Management Strategy As part of the capital strategy, I enabled NVIDIA to increase our investment in foundational models and datacentre AI offerings. Rather than distributing excess capital via large buybacks, capital was directed toward targeted acquisitions and strategic equity stakes in AI startups using NVIDIA infrastructure, ensuring ecosystem lock in. The capital allocation framework prioritised our Research and Development spend on inference optimisation, ML model compression, and next generation GPU architectures. Our balance sheet will show high resilience while maintaining top tier supply chain credit terms. In order to protect and expand the moat (Helmer, 2016), this strategy has created long term financial flexibility to deepen NVIDIA's entrenchment in core sectors such as health, robotics, cloud and digital twin integration. I was inspired by how ex-CEO Alan Mulally safeguarded Ford during the 2008 crisis by boldly mortgaging the company's assets to build a financial cushion (Feigen and Rosenberg, 2023). That lesson encouraged me to think differently about preparing NVIDIA for uncertainty, not from a place of fear, but to stay competitive and keep innovating even during challenging times. This means ensuring we have flexible funding options, like keeping a strong cash reserve, exploring long-term financing at favourable terms, and focusing our resources by possibly selling off non-essential parts of the business. It has been about staying agile and future-ready without weakening our financial foundation. Ensuring Effective Governance

Inspired by my peer Judy Marks CEO of Otis, I defined further our governance on "what we can control" (Edgecliffe-Johnson, 2024), I have focused on ensuring effective crisis governance by reinforcing agile management and decisive leadership. This involved scenario planning, rapid-response teams, and clear operational priorities to handle threats like DeepSeek. Transparent structures and real-time performance tracking would support quick, informed decisions without losing sight of long-term goals. Leadership should remain visible, and values driven. Like Marks, I have maintained open communication through regular updates and engagement across all levels to secure stability and trust. Upholding integrity, through data ethics, sustainability, and principled innovation, reinforces NVIDIA's credibility and resilience, positioning it as a responsible leader amid disruption. A key priority was to protect the board's independence and improve transparency. This included redesigning internal reporting dashboards and restoring board committee flows for capital spend, ethics, and innovation risk.

135

Post transition, we reconfigured to include ESG principles on AI ethics and quantum computing expertise. New directors I appointed have brought backgrounds in sustainable manufacturing scale, essential for NVIDIA's global ambitions. Governance frameworks were reviewed to strengthen enterprise risk management, with stricter standards over AI security, LLM misuse, and platform dependence risks. Building Trust and Confidence with Investors and Stakeholders Investor confidence was a central priority during leadership transition. With the stock having tripled over a short period, expectations were high. The investor relations team adopted a communication model, emphasising the defensibility of the platform through switching costs (Helmer, 2016). The vision of NVIDIA as an AI operating layer for global infrastructure was reinforced across earnings calls and investor summits. One of the most challenging times I faced as a CEO was the sudden drop of the shares value of NVIDA following the announcement from DeepSeek in China of the performance metrics. The stock value suddenly dropped from which was a major contrast with respect to the previous 18 months of performance (Macrotrends, 2025), shown at figure 2. Despite we lost USD 600 Billion in Market Capitalisation, I decided to recognise DeepSeek publicly as an 'excellent AI advancement' (Barlow and Krol, 2025) this was a major sign of integrity for NVIDIA.

Figure 2. 2 years of shares market value, emphasising the drop of value on January 27 2025 (Macrotrends, 2025)

To retain the confidence with investors, I called for a major shareholder global meeting a few days after the new. The key message was to keep faith in our AI project (Brustein, 2025) but emphasised on our strengths and future vision. A 93% year-over-year growth in data centre revenue demonstrates robust demand, while continued innovation, such as our upcoming Blackwell chips (NVIDIA, 2024b), signals strategic direction. Transparent communication and strong partnerships with cloud and tech firms further confirmed NVIDIA's central role in the AI ecosystem, reinforcing confidence in its long-term resilience and market leadership. 136

Furthermore, our executive board approved my plan on reinforcing two strategic powers: Branding and Process Power (Helmer, 2016), see figure 3. By strengthening its brand as the trusted leader in AI infrastructure, NVIDIA has obtained market leadership and long-term relevance. This includes clear messaging around product reliability, performance, and its unique developer ecosystem, which builds loyalty and reassures stakeholders. At the same time, leveraging Process Power requires refining core capabilities like chip design, integration, and time-to-market speed. These internal strengths are difficult to replicate and provide a lasting advantage, signalling that NVIDIA remains both innovative and operationally resilient in the face of external challenges.

Figure 3. Leveraging critical powers for NVIDIA at the Power Progression Curve (Helmer, 2016)

Strengthening Personal Leadership and Decision Making

This leadership journey began with humility, recognising that succeeding a founder required respect for legacy and a readiness to redefine the future. A structured decision-making model was adopted, combining stakeholder mapping, scenario planning, and intuitive judgement. Guided by Porter and Nohria (2018), I prioritised time for high-impact activities that strengthen leadership, strategy, team alignment, and relationship-building. Deliberate time was invested in learning from internal engineers and global partners. I formed a personal leadership circle of advisers in AI policy, deep tech, and national security, which helped shape NVIDIA's positions on AI safety and regulatory engagement. Consistent with Porter and Nohria's research, my approach focused on integrating diverse perspectives into bold, pragmatic decisions.

Conclusion

Leading NVIDIA through this transformative phase has demanded a careful balance of continuity and renewal. Succeeding a visionary founder meant not only preserving strategic strengths, but also reshaping leadership for an era defined by rapid innovation and fierce competition. By applying frameworks such as Helmer's strategic powers and the CEO framework from Feigen Advisors, I was able to guide the company through challenges including the emergence of DeepSeek. Strategic clarity, resilient capital allocation, and governance reform have played a pivotal role in strengthening NVIDIA's foundations. Rebuilding investor trust required transparency, humility, and a renewed emphasis on brand value and internal capabilities. Moreover, the emphasis on talent, decentralised innovation, and ethical leadership ensured that NVIDIA remained agile and future-focused. As AI continues to reshape the global landscape, our longterm success will depend not only on technology, but on the integrity, judgement, and adaptability of our leadership. This journey has reaffirmed my belief that purposeful leadership, grounded in strategic insight and collaborative learning, is essential for sustaining both growth and trust in times of disruption.

This assignment is intended to provide an opportunity to integrate the material from this module by applying it to a real-world organisation. It is also designed to improve such important managerial skills as: project management, report writing and analysis. Groups are required to identify one core strategy challenge in an existing organisation of their choosing, for-profit or non-for-profit, and to analyse and propose ways to address this challenge using the concepts, models, frameworks and tools introduced and discussed in class and in the essential reading. The chosen organisation must have a minimum of ten (10) employees. Groups are NOT ALLOWED to write about an organisation extensively discussed in this and other Cambridge MBA modules, or in which one of the group members currently works or worked immediately prior to joining the Cambridge MBA. They are encouraged to discuss their choice of organisation with the course leader and/or teaching assistant. It is not necessary to have direct access to the organisation. Groups may choose an organisation that is currently in the news, as long as they can gather enough information to develop a compelling analysis. Although not every one of the concepts, models, frameworks and tools introduced and discussed in class and in the essential reading may be needed or appropriate for the analysis of the identified strategic challenge and chosen organisation, the assignment will be expected to integrate a broad array of relevant concepts and approaches. Assignments should take into consideration and show a good understanding of the following elements:

The core strategy challenge should be identified and discussed as appropriate. Relevant and systematically referenced data should support all statements and analyses. Furthermore, the analysis should offer a realistic and coherent way forward, and explain why, how and when the organisation should address the identified challenge. For instance, by changing its existing business strategy, diversifying into new markets and/or offerings, or getting into a merger or strategic alliance (if so, with whom and where).

Strategic Analysis: Applying Blue Ocean Strategy to NVIDIA NVIDIA, a global leader in graphics processing units (GPUs), artificial intelligence (AI), and highperformance computing, operates within a rapidly evolving and highly competitive technology landscape. Its influence extends across core markets including gaming, data centres, professional visualisation, and automotive solutions. While NVIDIA has consistently led through technological innovation, it faces a significant strategic challenge: overreliance on the GPU market, which is increasingly saturated and vulnerable to intense pricing pressure, technological convergence, and geopolitical constraints. This analysis proposes that NVIDIA address this core challenge by applying the principles of Blue Ocean Strategy, as outlined by Kim and Mauborgne (2015). Unlike traditional strategies that focus on outperforming competitors in existing markets, Blue Ocean Strategy advocates the creation of uncontested market space. This requires shifting from a red ocean of intense rivalry to a blue ocean where competition becomes irrelevant. The strategic question facing NVIDIA is how to reduce its dependence on intensifying competition in GPU markets while leveraging its capabilities to enter new arenas. NVIDIA has already taken preliminary steps in this direction through the development of Omniverse, a real-time 3D simulation and collaboration platform. However, this platform remains underutilised and under-commercialised, particularly in enterprise and industrial applications. The proposal is for 141

NVIDIA to reposition Omniverse as the foundation of a broader Simulation-as-a-Service platform targeting industries such as logistics, healthcare, urban planning, and advanced manufacturing. This move would allow NVIDIA to move beyond hardware dependence and generate new streams of recurring software revenue. Applying the Four Actions Framework from Blue Ocean Strategy provides a structured method for reimagining NVIDIA's strategic direction. First, the firm should eliminate its narrow focus on hardware performance benchmarks as a primary differentiator, especially in the gaming segment. Second, it should reduce its overinvestment in incremental GPU improvements that are yielding diminishing returns. Third, NVIDIA must raise its commitment to developing integrated software and AI solutions tailored to industry-specific simulation needs. Lastly, and most critically, the company should create a new offering by transforming Omniverse into a full-stack platform for building and operating digital twins in the enterprise space. This strategy fits within the broader ecosystem in which NVIDIA operates. The firm already possesses a strong foundation of AI frameworks, developer tools, and partnerships with cloud providers such as Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services. Leveraging these existing assets, NVIDIA can position Omniverse as a platform that allows clients to develop, test, and deploy simulations across diverse domains. For instance, urban planners could simulate traffic flow using real-time data, manufacturers could optimise factory layouts virtually, and healthcare providers could train medical professionals in a risk-free environment. From a governance perspective, implementing this strategic shift would require the formation of a dedicated division reporting directly to senior leadership. This division should focus on product development, ecosystem engagement, and industry partnerships. Performance indicators must be aligned with adoption rates, ecosystem growth, and recurring revenue generation. The business model would evolve from primarily transactional sales of hardware to a Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) model featuring tiered pricing, marketplace integration, and co-development opportunities with enterprise partners. The benefits of this strategic transformation are multifaceted. Firstly, it allows NVIDIA to escape the cyclical nature of the hardware business by creating a recurring revenue stream. Secondly, it positions the company at the forefront of digital transformation in critical industries. Thirdly, it enhances the stickiness of the NVIDIA ecosystem, making it more difficult for competitors to displace its solutions. As Grant (2022) notes, firms that integrate resources into platforms and ecosystems are more likely to generate sustainable competitive advantage in dynamic environments. Nevertheless, this strategy is not without risks. Adoption rates may be slow if enterprises lack the digital maturity or technical skills to implement simulation platforms effectively. There is also the challenge of shifting internal focus from product engineering to platform and service delivery. These risks can be mitigated by investing in user-friendly interfaces, offering onboarding and support services, and nurturing a developer community akin to NVIDIA's success with CUDA. Additionally, pilot partnerships with established firms in key industries can help demonstrate the value of Omniverse and accelerate credibility in new markets. Transparency and fairness, principles drawn from broader management literature, are critical in ensuring that such a transformation is accepted internally and externally. As Willink and Babin (2015) argue, extreme ownership and clarity in execution are essential for driving organisational change. Senior leaders must communicate the vision clearly, outline expectations, and align incentives to encourage cross-functional collaboration. Feedback mechanisms should be established to gather input from stakeholders and refine the offering iteratively. This strategic redirection also supports NVIDIA's long-term ambitions in AI and automation. By shifting from discrete hardware products to integrated platforms, NVIDIA reinforces its role as an enabler of next-generation computing solutions. Moreover, the move aligns with global trends towards digital twins, smart cities, and AI-driven automation. Rumelt's (2011) insistence on coherent action is evident in this approach: it connects market insights, organisational capabilities, and execution pathways into a unified direction.

142

In conclusion, NVIDIA's strategic challenge of overdependence on a highly competitive GPU market can be effectively addressed through the application of Blue Ocean Strategy. By leveraging its existing assets to create a new market for AI-driven simulation platforms, the company can unlock uncontested growth opportunities. This approach requires a fundamental shift in mindset, business model, and internal alignment, but the potential rewards in terms of market leadership, resilience, and innovation are substantial. If executed with discipline and ownership, this strategic pivot can define NVIDIA's next phase of growth and ensure its continued relevance in a rapidly transforming technological landscape.

BUT private credit is attractive to specialised investors with in-depth knowledge and the ability to oversee private credit funds effectively | 31

Recommendations

Best Practices for Institutional Investors Moving Forward with Private Credit Define a clear strategic rationale  ASRS has a philosophy to address disequilibria in public and private markets  SERS articulates core reason for investing in private credit: achieve attractive risk-adjusted returns and higher yield through illiquidity premium

Aim for long-term capital appreciation  Longer-term perspective allows full realisation of the illiquidity premium, enabling funds to weather short-term turmoil  Longer horizons mean lower need for riskier trades and higher leverage

Focus on governance, compliance, monitoring  Asset owners must regulate themselves to ensure strong governance  Consistent audits and external oversight may help ensure that processes are followed

Utilise strength to push for improvements  All asset owners should focus on increased transparency  Large investors, e.g. pension and insurance funds, should use asset strength to push for better fees, reporting and controls

Letter formatted as Assignment for JBS: AI financial advice: helpful tool or dangerous shortcut? An investigation into ChatGPT's financial advice capabilities reveals both promise and peril in AI personal finance (The Guardian, 2025a). While the chatbot provided "decent" pension guidance, its mortgage advice was dismissed as "not even close" to qualified advice, highlighting urgent regulatory concerns. The Guardian's experts noted ChatGPT's mortgage advice ignored crucial factors like borrower criteria and alternative deal structures. This superficial analysis could lead consumers into inappropriate financial products, given AI's tendency to present incomplete information with unwarranted confidence. Insurance brokers described responses as "very generic" and failing to account for policy complexities. These limitations become concerning when consumers may not recognise gaps in AI-generated advice. The risks extend beyond individual consumers. The Bank of England has warned about AI driven market manipulation (The Guardian, 2025b). If AI systems designed for institutional trading can "exploit weaknesses" and trigger market volatility, what safeguards exist for consumer-facing AI? The Bank of England emphasised that AI tools must operate within existing regulatory frameworks when providing financial guidance (Bank of England, 2024). Yet ChatGPT's pension calculations contained basic errors, including incorrect state pension age information. If millions rely on flawed advice, could we face widespread retirement disasters? The European Securities and Markets Authority provided guidance emphasising that firms using AI in investment services must maintain appropriate oversight and transparency (European Securities and Markets Authority, 2024). While The Guardian concludes AI serves as a useful starting point, the gap between ChatGPT's confident presentation and expert criticism suggests consumers may not recognise these limitations. Financial authorities must clarify whether AI platforms providing financial guidance require authorisation and mandate clear disclaimers; stakes are too high for "learn as we go" approach. Notes: The letter was followed by my full name and contact information, but it has been removed since the cover page for this assignment required Student Blind Grade Number. References were included as hyperlinks following the format of published letters in the website of the newspaper. Harvard Style citations are added in the version above to make it consistent with the assignments at JBS. 300 words max. was The Guardian limit. Original Version of the letter sent is shown in the Appendix Section.

OP-ED to Financial Times Emerging Market Currencies - The Opportunity in the Eye of the Storm An Analytical Perspective on Risk and Reward There is growing debate over the rise of emerging market currencies during this period of global turbulence. Yet for those of us at the crossroads of banking, investment and artificial intelligence, this moment signals potential rather than peril. As fund managers pull back from the dollar amid erratic US policy shifts, strong and resilient currencies from the developing world are stepping forward. Far from fragile, many are outperforming their counterparts in supposedly stable economies (Cotterill & Herbert, 2025). This is more than a passing phase. It marks a shift in how capital is allocated and risk interpreted. Banks and investors embracing analytics and modern tools are gaining a clear advantage. The real question is not whether these currencies are risky, but whether we can evaluate that risk wisely. The evidence says we can. A Market Understood Through Auction Theory To understand what is happening, let's consider auction theory, especially the work of Nobel Prize winners Paul Milgrom and Robert Wilson (Nobel Prize Committee, 2020). Their research into how markets function with uneven information helps explain why some investors are now identifying untapped value in emerging markets. These are not empty hopes. They are grounded in opportunity. Yet because many models have not adapted, investment remains below potential. Emerging market equities accounted for 8 percent of global equity fund holdings in 2017. That has dropped to just 5 percent (Cotterill & Herbert, 2025). This decline stems more from hesitation than from a change in fundamentals. Amartya Sen, the Economics Nobel laureate from University of Cambridge, offered another way to frame this. In Development as Freedom, he argued that real development should be measured by capabilities, not simply output (Sen, 1999). While wealthier economies debate monetary tightening, many emerging countries have quietly strengthened their institutions, digitised systems and diversified trade. These are signs of growing maturity. AI-Driven Insights from Latin America Latin America shows how these markets are adapting. In 2024, Colombia's central bank launched AI tools to improve forecasting of currency movements. These models draw on data from pricing, trade and markets to assess financial risks more accurately (Rowland, 2024). 164

AI does not remove uncertainty, but it helps interpret it. Machine learning can detect complex relationships between commodity flows, interest rates and global investment trends. The result is better valuations and stronger confidence in decision-making. Strategic Implications for Banking There are risks nevertheless; the Bank of England's 2024 Financial Stability Report noted that volatility in emerging market currencies could affect UK institutions (Bank of England, 2024). But risk cuts both ways. Banks with the right tools and local insight can turn instability into opportunity. A UK business sourcing materials from Vietnam or Brazil, for instance, can take out loans in local currency, aligning debt with expenses. This approach reduces exposure to currency swings and enhances predictability. It is important to highlight that the IMF reports a 4 percent fall in emerging market currencies against the dollar this year, but that average conceals a wide gap between countries with strong fundamentals and those without (Adrian, Natalucci & Wu, 2024). Zooming out, the International Monetary Fund forecasts that emerging markets will grow by 4.2 percent in 2024 and 2025. Developed economies are expected to grow at half that rate or less (International Monetary Fund, 2025). This is not wishful thinking. It reflects better fiscal management, maturing institutions and real productivity. A Call to Action It is time to shed the outdated mindset that emerging market currencies are inherently risky. With stronger fundamentals and clearer data, they are increasingly stable assets. The path forward is not speculation but careful analysis. Financial institutions must invest in region-specific expertise, embrace AI-powered risk models and design solutions tailored to the realities of these economies. The reward lies not only in performance, but in resilience and long-term growth. Emerging market currencies are not the eye of the storm. They are the centre of a new global order. The opportunity is clear. The moment to act is now. Sincerely, MBA Student, Judge Business School, University of Cambridge (Name to be provided in OP-ED to FT. - Anonymised following JBS Guidelines)

APPENDIX III – Letter to be Sent to FT (in case OP-Ed is not published) Word count: 375 The Financial Times' recent coverage of the resilience of emerging market currencies shines a necessary light on a crucial but often misunderstood global shift (Cotterill & Herbert, 2025). While headlines focus on dollar volatility and interest rate uncertainty, the real story is the quiet strength of emerging economies. This is not about exotic risk, but strategic opportunity. As global capital begins to pivot away from the dollar, many emerging market currencies are outperforming their developed counterparts. It is a wake-up call to rethink what constitutes safety and value in today's world. Nobel laureates Paul Milgrom and Robert Wilson taught us that market outcomes are shaped by private knowledge and bidding dynamics (Nobel Prize Committee, 2020). Today, investors are waking up to the "private value" embedded in emerging economies, whose assets remain undervalued. Since 2017, emerging market stocks have fallen from 8 to just 5 percent of global equity fund holdings, a mispricing that savvy investors are beginning to correct. Development is not merely about GDP. Amartya Sen's vision of "development as freedom" still holds weight (Sen, 1999). Many of these economies have invested in institutions and capabilities, while developed nations remain mired in policy gridlock. Colombia offers a vivid example. In 2024, its central bank adopted artificial intelligence to improve exchange rate forecasting, a clear leap forward in monetary planning and financial transparency (Rowland, 2024). These tools enhance confidence and make investing in such currencies far more appealing. However, IMF reports a 4 percent fall in emerging market currencies against the dollar this year, but that average conceals a wide gap between countries with strong fundamentals and those without (Adrian, Natalucci & Wu, 2024). For British companies with ties to Vietnam, Mexico or beyond, emerging market currencies are not a risk to be feared but a natural hedge. Aligning revenues and costs in local currency reduces exposure and smooths volatility. With growth projected at 4.2 percent for emerging economies, double that of developed markets (International Monetary Fund, 2025), the question is no longer whether to act, but how soon? Through systematic application of Voice of the Customer, Gage R&R, Root Cause Analysis, Design of Experiments, and Control Charts, the process addressed every aspect from initial requirements gathering to ongoing performance validation. This comprehensive methodology ensured the Python/R-Shiny platform delivered the 100% accuracy requirement essential for multiyear research projects. Voice of the Customer captured genuine researcher needs, whilst Gage R&R validated measurement system reliability before implementation. Root Cause Analysis identified fundamental workflow limitations, DOE optimised platform parameters systematically, and Control Charts provided continuous performance monitoring. This systematic approach eliminated assumptions and ensured evidence-based decision making throughout platform development. The DMADV methodology successfully transformed the forex analysis workflow from manual, timeintensive processes to an automated, research-grade platform that prioritised accuracy over speed. By following this structured approach, the resulting system met rigorous academic standards whilst enhancing visualisation capabilities and data processing efficiency. This foundation enabled sustainable analytical improvements and supported the long-term research objectives essential for comprehensive forex market analysis.
